scenarios.title: Every button does the same thing
scenarios.situation: A teammate generates five callbacks in a loop. Every callback prints 4, no matter which one is called.
scenarios.prompt: Why do all the callbacks behave identically, and how do you fix it?
evidence:
handlers = [lambda: print(i) for i in range(5)]
handlers[0]()  # prints 4
handlers[2]()  # prints 4
choices: The lambda captures the variable i itself, not its value at creation — bind it with a default argument
List comprehensions share one lambda object — use a for loop with append instead
print buffers output — flush after each call
range(5) yields the same object five times — use list(range(5))
scenarios.why: Closures capture variables by reference, not values. When any handler runs, it looks up the current value of i, which is 4 after the loop finished. Binding the value at definition time — lambda i=i: print(i) — gives each callback its own copy.
scenarios.hint: When is the value of i actually looked up: when the lambda is defined, or when it is called?

scenarios.title: The disappearing cent
scenarios.situation: A billing helper splits a dollar amount in cents evenly, but the ledger is off by a cent on some invoices.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the split, and which operator fixes it?
evidence:
def split_cents(total_cents, n):
    share = total_cents / n
    return [round(share)] * n

split_cents(100, 3)  # [33, 33, 33] -> sums to 99
choices: round() uses banker's rounding — use math.ceil instead
/ produces a float and the remainder cent is silently dropped — use divmod for quotient and remainder
List multiplication shares one int object — build the list with a comprehension
Integers are immutable — the shares cannot be adjusted after creation
scenarios.why: Floating-point division plus rounding discards the remainder: 100/3 rounds to 33 three times, totaling 99. divmod(100, 3) returns (33, 1), letting you distribute the leftover cent explicitly so the shares always sum to the original total.
scenarios.hint: Where does the missing cent go? Which builtin returns both the quotient and the remainder at once?

scenarios.title: Works in the REPL, fails in production
scenarios.situation: A role check passes during manual testing but rejects admin users when the value comes from an HTTP request body.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the check behave differently, and what is the correct comparison?
choices: is compares object identity, not value — runtime-built strings are different objects, so use ==
JSON strings are bytes — decode before comparing
Request data is lazily evaluated — call request.get_json(force=True)
String interning is disabled in production — enable it with sys.intern
scenarios.why: The is operator tests whether two names point to the same object in memory. CPython interns some string literals, which is why the check accidentally works in the REPL, but a string parsed from JSON is a distinct object with equal value. Value comparison with == is the correct test.
scenarios.hint: What exactly does is test — the characters in the string, or something about the objects themselves?

scenarios.title: The cache that never hits
scenarios.situation: A lookup helper accepts an optional cache dict. Profiling shows the expensive computation runs on every call even when a cache is passed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the bug in the cache check?
choices: not cache is True for an empty dict, so a legitimately empty cache is thrown away every call — test cache is None instead
Default arguments are evaluated once — use a module-level dict
Dicts are unordered — the key lookup misses on ordering
None is falsy — the check should be if cache == {}
scenarios.why: Empty containers are falsy, so `not cache` is True both when no cache was passed (None) and when an empty dict was passed. The caller's empty dict gets discarded and replaced, so entries never accumulate. Testing `cache is None` distinguishes 'not provided' from 'provided but empty'.
scenarios.hint: List every value that makes `not cache` True. Which of those are legitimate caches?

scenarios.title: 2.67 is not 2.67
scenarios.situation: A totals report formats currency with round(x, 2), but a price of 2.675 renders as 2.67 and reconciliation fails.
scenarios.prompt: Why does rounding misbehave here, and what type should money use?
choices: round() has a bug with .5 fractions — file an issue and use string slicing
2.675 cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point (it stores as 2.67499...) — use decimal.Decimal for money
f-strings truncate instead of rounding — use format(x, '.2f')
Python rounds toward zero — use math.floor with an offset
scenarios.why: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly; the stored value of 2.675 is actually slightly less, so it rounds down. This is inherent to IEEE 754 doubles, not a bug. The decimal module represents decimal fractions exactly and is the standard choice for currency.
scenarios.hint: What base does a float use internally, and can 2.675 be written exactly in that base?

scenarios.title: The condition that never fires
scenarios.situation: A notification helper is only supposed to escalate when sending fails, but the escalation branch never executes.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the failure branch dead code?
choices: Functions without a return statement return None, which is falsy — the helper must return a success flag
print returns the string — compare against the message instead
if treats missing returns as True — invert the condition
The function raises before returning — wrap the call in try/except
scenarios.why: Every Python function returns None unless it executes a return with a value. The if statement therefore always sees a falsy value. Side-effect helpers should either return an explicit status the caller can test, or be called for their effect alone without a condition.
scenarios.hint: What value does a function produce when execution simply falls off the end of the body?

scenarios.title: Counting words the slow way
scenarios.situation: A log analyzer counts word frequencies with a hand-rolled loop and an if/else on every word. It works but is verbose and slow to read.
scenarios.prompt: Which stdlib tool replaces the manual loop most idiomatically?
choices: collections.Counter — counts = Counter(words), then counts.most_common(10)
collections.deque — popleft is O(1) for the top words
array.array — stores the counts in a typed C array
functools.reduce — fold the words into a dict in one expression
scenarios.why: Counter is a dict subclass built exactly for frequency counting; its constructor consumes an iterable and most_common(n) returns the n highest counts without a manual sort. The hand-rolled loop reimplements what the stdlib already provides, tested and optimized.
scenarios.hint: Which collections class is literally a dict subclass designed for counting hashable items?

scenarios.title: The 2 GB list nobody needed
scenarios.situation: A CSV pipeline loads every row into a list, transforms it, then iterates once to write output. The job OOMs on large files.
scenarios.prompt: What is the minimal change that fixes the memory blowup?
choices: Replace the list comprehension with a generator expression so rows are produced lazily, one at a time
Call gc.collect() inside the loop to free each row sooner
Convert rows to a tuple — tuples use less memory than lists
Read the file in binary mode to halve the memory footprint
scenarios.why: A list comprehension materializes every element at once, while a generator expression — (transform(r) for r in read_csv(...)) — yields each row on demand and discards it after use. Since the pipeline consumes rows exactly once, laziness cuts peak memory from O(n) to O(1) per row.
scenarios.hint: The data is consumed exactly once, in order. Does it all need to exist in memory at the same time?

scenarios.title: TypeError: unhashable type
scenarios.situation: A config loader builds a dict keyed by coordinate pairs, but crashes with TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the key fail, and what is the correct key type?
choices: Dict keys must be hashable and immutable in practice — use the tuple (x, y) as the key
Dict keys must be strings — use f"{x},{y}"
Lists cannot be dict keys on 64-bit Python — switch to a 32-bit build
The dict needs a default factory — use defaultdict(list)
scenarios.why: Dict lookup hashes the key, and lists are mutable so Python makes them unhashable — a key whose hash could change would corrupt the table. Tuples are immutable and hashable (when their contents are), so (x, y) is the natural key for a coordinate pair.
scenarios.hint: What property must a dict key have so its hash stays valid for the lifetime of the entry?

scenarios.title: The queue that gets slower as it grows
scenarios.situation: A task queue is a plain list; workers pop(0) to take the next job. Latency climbs linearly with queue length.
scenarios.prompt: Why does pop(0) degrade, and which structure fixes it?
evidence:
jobs = [...100k items...]
while jobs:
    job = jobs.pop(0)  # gets slower over time
    handle(job)
choices: pop(0) shifts every remaining element, making it O(n) — use collections.deque, whose popleft() is O(1)
Lists store pointers — convert to array.array for contiguous storage
pop(0) triggers a full garbage collection — disable gc during the loop
While loops are slow — rewrite with a for loop over the list
scenarios.why: Removing from the front of a list memmoves all remaining elements down one slot, so each pop costs O(n) and the whole drain costs O(n²). A deque is a doubly-linked block structure with O(1) appends and pops on both ends — the right tool for FIFO queues.
scenarios.hint: What has to physically happen to the other 99,999 elements when the first one is removed from a contiguous array?

scenarios.title: Dedup that scrambles the order
scenarios.situation: A teammate deduplicates a list of user IDs with set(), but downstream code depends on first-seen order and starts failing.
scenarios.prompt: How do you deduplicate while preserving first-seen order?
evidence:
ids = [7, 3, 7, 1, 3, 9]
unique = list(set(ids))  # order lost: [1, 3, 7, 9] or arbitrary
choices: list(dict.fromkeys(ids)) — dicts preserve insertion order and drop duplicate keys
sorted(set(ids)) — sorting restores the original order
list(ids).remove duplicates with a nested loop checking index()
Use frozenset instead of set — frozensets preserve order
scenarios.why: Sets are unordered by design, so converting through one discards the original sequence. Since Python 3.7 dicts preserve insertion order, dict.fromkeys(ids) keeps the first occurrence of each ID and drops later duplicates, and list() converts back.
scenarios.hint: Which builtin mapping both rejects duplicate keys and remembers the order keys were first inserted?

scenarios.title: Rows of uneven length
scenarios.situation: A CSV parser unpacks each row into fixed variables, but some rows carry extra trailing columns and crash with ValueError: too many values to unpack.
scenarios.prompt: How do you unpack the first columns and collect the rest without knowing the row length?
evidence:
for row in reader:
    name, age, city = row  # ValueError on rows with 4+ columns
choices: Use starred unpacking: name, age, city, *extra = row — extra collects the remainder as a list
Slice first: name, age, city = row[0], row[1], row[2]
Wrap in try/except ValueError and skip malformed rows
Pad every row to the max length with None before unpacking
scenarios.why: Extended unpacking with a starred target captures any number of leftover items into a list, so name, age, city, *extra = row works for rows of length 3 or more. It expresses 'first three, plus the rest' directly instead of manual slicing.
scenarios.hint: Which unpacking syntax lets one target absorb a variable number of leftover items?

scenarios.title: The growing default list
scenarios.situation: A helper collects validation errors, defaulting to a fresh list per call — except callers who omit the argument see errors from previous calls.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause, and what is the correct fix?
choices: Default arguments are evaluated once at def time, so every call shares one list — default to None and create the list inside
Lists are passed by reference — callers must pass errors[:] to copy
append is not atomic — protect it with a threading lock
The function is recursive — the list accumulates across frames
scenarios.why: Python evaluates default argument expressions once, when the def statement runs. The single list object is then reused as the default for every call. The standard fix is errors=None with `if errors is None: errors = []` inside the body, creating a fresh list per call.
scenarios.hint: When does Python evaluate a default argument value — each call, or once?

scenarios.title: The wrapper that drops arguments
scenarios.situation: A timing wrapper works on simple functions but crashes with TypeError when applied to a function that takes keyword arguments.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from the wrapper?
choices: The wrapper accepts *args but not **kwargs, so keyword arguments have nowhere to go — add **kwargs and forward them
Decorators cannot wrap functions with defaults — remove the default value
time.perf_counter is monotonic — use time.time instead
The wrapper must be defined with functools.partial, not a nested def
scenarios.why: A transparent wrapper must accept everything the wrapped function accepts. *args captures positional arguments only; without **kwargs, any keyword argument raises TypeError. The fix is def wrapper(*args, **kwargs) with fn(*args, **kwargs).
scenarios.hint: Where do the keyword arguments go when the wrapper's signature has no parameter that can receive them?

scenarios.title: The decorator that erases identity
scenarios.situation: After adding a logging decorator, stack traces and help() show wrapper instead of the real function names, confusing on-call debugging.
scenarios.prompt: How do you make a decorator preserve the wrapped function's metadata?
choices: Apply @functools.wraps(fn) to the inner wrapper — it copies __name__, __doc__, and __module__
Assign wrapper.__name__ = fn.__name__ manually at the end of the decorator
Decorators cannot preserve metadata — remove the decorator in production
Use a class-based decorator instead of a function-based one
scenarios.why: functools.wraps updates the wrapper's __name__, __qualname__, __doc__, __dict__, and __module__ from the wrapped function, so introspection, tracebacks, and documentation tools see the original. Manual assignment works for __name__ alone but misses the rest.
scenarios.hint: Which stdlib decorator exists specifically to copy a wrapped function's metadata onto its wrapper?

scenarios.title: ModuleNotFoundError on a file that exists
scenarios.situation: A script imports a sibling helper module. It runs from the project root but fails with ModuleNotFoundError when launched from a subdirectory.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the import depend on the working directory, and what is the robust fix?
evidence:
$ cd scripts && python cleanup.py
Traceback: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'helpers'
choices: Python resolves top-level imports against sys.path, which includes the script's directory but not the project root — run as a module (python -m) or structure the code as a package
Helper modules must be installed with pip before any script can import them
Python caches imports per directory — delete __pycache__ and retry
Relative imports are required — change to from . import helpers
scenarios.why: The script's own directory is placed on sys.path, not the caller's working directory or the project root. Launching from elsewhere changes what 'helpers' resolves to. Organizing the code as a package and running python -m project.scripts.cleanup from the root makes imports location-independent.
scenarios.hint: Which directories does Python actually search for a top-level import, and which of those changed?

scenarios.title: RecursionError on deep input
scenarios.situation: A recursive tree walker handles test fixtures fine but crashes with RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded on a production dataset.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right response to hitting the recursion limit?
choices: Rewrite iteratively with an explicit stack — raising the recursion limit just moves the crash to a stack overflow
Call sys.setrecursionlimit(10**9) at startup to remove the ceiling
Convert the function to a generator — generators have no recursion limit
Add @functools.lru_cache so repeated subtrees are not revisited
scenarios.why: The limit (default 1000) guards the C stack; each Python frame consumes C stack space, so raising the limit risks a hard segfault instead of a catchable error. An explicit list-based stack converts the traversal to iteration with heap-allocated memory, which scales to arbitrary depth.
scenarios.hint: What resource does each recursive call consume, and does raising the limit create more of it?

scenarios.title: The same three arguments, everywhere
scenarios.situation: Dozens of call sites repeat requests.get(url, timeout=30, headers=AUTH_HEADERS). A teammate wants one place to change the defaults.
scenarios.prompt: Which tool creates the specialized callable with the least boilerplate?
choices: functools.partial(requests.get, timeout=30, headers=AUTH_HEADERS) — a callable with those arguments pre-filled
A lambda: lambda url: requests.get(url, timeout=30, headers=AUTH_HEADERS)
functools.reduce to fold the repeated arguments into one call
A module-level global TIMEOUT that each call site reads
scenarios.why: functools.partial returns a new callable with positional and keyword arguments frozen in, so api_get(url) expands to the full call. It preserves introspection better than a lambda and keeps the preset arguments in exactly one place.
scenarios.hint: Which stdlib helper builds a new callable from an old one with some arguments already filled in?

scenarios.title: Every cart shares one basket
scenarios.situation: A ShoppingCart class defines items = [] at class level. Customers report seeing other shoppers' items in their carts.
scenarios.prompt: Why do instances share state, and how do you give each cart its own list?
evidence:
class ShoppingCart:
    items = []  # class attribute
    def add(self, item):
        self.items.append(item)

c1, c2 = ShoppingCart(), ShoppingCart()
c1.add("book")
print(c2.items)  # ['book'] -- leaked
choices: items is a class attribute — one list shared by all instances; assign self.items = [] in __init__
append mutates in place — use self.items = self.items + [item]
Class attributes are read-only — move the list to a module global
Instances need deepcopy — copy the list in add()
scenarios.why: Attributes defined directly in the class body belong to the class object, and self.items.append mutates that single shared list rather than creating per-instance state. Initializing self.items = [] inside __init__ gives every instance its own list.
scenarios.hint: Whose list is being appended to — the instance's, or an object they all have in common?

scenarios.title: The subclass that forgot its parents
scenarios.situation: A subclass defines its own __init__ and sets new fields, but inherited methods crash with AttributeError on attributes the base class normally sets.
choices: The subclass never called super().__init__(color), so the base-class attributes were never initialized
Subclasses cannot add parameters — remove radius from the signature
color must be a class attribute — define it on Shape directly
Python requires __init__ chaining via Shape.__init__(self, color) only, never super()
scenarios.why: Defining __init__ in a subclass replaces the base version entirely; base-class initialization only happens if the subclass explicitly cooperates via super().__init__(...). Without it, any attribute the base __init__ sets is missing on subclass instances.
scenarios.hint: What runs when you define __init__ in the subclass — the base version, the subclass version, or both?

scenarios.title: Duplicates in the set
scenarios.situation: A Product class implements __eq__ so equal SKUs compare equal, yet a set of products still holds duplicates.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the set ignore the custom equality?
choices: Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None, so the objects hash by identity — implement __hash__ consistent with __eq__
Sets use == only for strings — products need a custom set subclass
The __eq__ signature is wrong — it must accept *args
__eq__ is only called by ==, never by containers — use a dict instead
scenarios.why: Set membership hashes the object first and only calls __eq__ on hash collisions. When a class defines __eq__ without __hash__, Python sets __hash__ to None, making instances unhashable-by-value — they fall back to identity hashing, so equal SKUs land in different buckets. The rule: objects that compare equal must hash equal.
scenarios.hint: What does a set check before it ever calls __eq__?

scenarios.title: Validation that runs once
scenarios.situation: A BankAccount validates the opening balance in __init__, but later assignments like acct.balance = -50 bypass validation silently.
scenarios.prompt: How do you enforce the invariant on every assignment?
choices: Expose balance as a @property with a setter that validates — every assignment routes through the setter
Override __setattr__ to intercept all attribute writes
Make balance private and add a set_balance method callers must use
Validate in __del__ so invalid states are caught at cleanup
scenarios.why: A property with a setter keeps attribute-style access (acct.balance = x) while routing every write through validation logic. __init__ should assign via self.balance too, so the single setter guards construction and later mutation alike.
scenarios.hint: Which mechanism lets attribute assignment syntax run custom code on every write?

scenarios.title: Which save() runs?
scenarios.situation: A class inherits from two mixins that both define save(). The wrong one executes, and reordering the base classes changes behavior.
scenarios.prompt: How does Python decide which save() runs, and how do you inspect the order?
choices: Python follows the Method Resolution Order (C3 linearization) — Record.__mro__ shows AuditMixin before CacheMixin, so its save() wins
The last base class always wins — CacheMixin.save should have run, so this is a bug
Mixins are merged alphabetically — AuditMixin wins by name
Both save() methods run — the observation must be a logging error
scenarios.why: Attribute lookup walks the class's MRO — the C3 linearization shown by __mro__ — and uses the first match. With (AuditMixin, CacheMixin), audit's save() shadows cache's. Cooperative mixins call super().save() so every mixin in the chain gets its turn.
scenarios.hint: What does Record.__mro__ print, and what does the first match in that sequence determine?

scenarios.title: Boilerplate __init__ and __repr__
scenarios.situation: A simple config holder needs __init__, __repr__, and __eq__. The hand-written versions are 30 lines and already have a copy-paste bug.
scenarios.prompt: Which stdlib feature generates these correctly?
evidence:
class DbConfig:
    def __init__(self, host, port=5432, tags=None):
        self.host = host
        self.port = port
        self.tags = tags if tags is not None else []
    def __repr__(self): ...  # 12 more lines
    def __eq__(self, other): ...  # 8 more lines
choices: @dataclass — generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from annotated fields; use field(default_factory=list) for the mutable default
@functools.total_ordering — generates the comparison methods from __lt__
collections.namedtuple — immutable and generates everything needed
typing.Protocol — declares the structural interface instead
scenarios.why: The dataclass decorator synthesizes __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from field annotations, eliminating the hand-written boilerplate where the bug lived. Mutable defaults must use field(default_factory=...) because a plain [] default would be shared — the same mutable-default rule as functions.
scenarios.hint: Which decorator turns annotated class variables into a generated __init__ and friends?

scenarios.title: The file left open on error
scenarios.situation: A report writer opens a file, writes rows, and closes it at the end — but a mid-loop exception leaves the file handle open and the output truncated.
scenarios.prompt: What construct guarantees the file is closed even when an exception strikes?
evidence:
f = open("report.csv", "w")
for row in rows:
    f.write(format(row))  # raises on row 900 of 1000
f.close()  # never reached
choices: A with statement — the context manager closes the file when the block exits, normally or via exception
A try/finally around the whole loop with f.close() in the finally
Opening in append mode so partial writes are preserved
Calling f.flush() after every write so nothing is lost
scenarios.why: with open(...) as f: ties the file's lifetime to the block: __exit__ closes the handle whether the block completes, raises, or returns. The manual open/close pattern leaks the handle on any early exit, and relying on the garbage collector to close files is implementation-specific and unreliable.
scenarios.hint: Which statement runs cleanup code automatically when its block is exited for any reason?

scenarios.title: TypeError: not JSON serializable
scenarios.situation: An API payload builder crashes when a datetime sneaks into the dict passed to json.dumps.
scenarios.prompt: How do you serialize values the json module does not natively support?
evidence:
payload = {"user": "amy", "at": datetime.now(timezone.utc)}
json.dumps(payload)  # TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable
choices: Pass default=str (or a custom function) to json.dumps so unsupported objects get a fallback conversion
Convert the payload with str(payload) and send that instead of JSON
Subclass dict to auto-convert datetimes on insertion
Use pickle instead of json — it serializes everything
scenarios.why: The json module only handles dict, list, str, int, float, bool, and None. Its default parameter is a function called for anything else — default=str converts datetimes via str(), while a custom function can emit isoformat() for precise round-tripping. pickle is not a substitute: it is Python-specific and unsafe on untrusted data.
scenarios.hint: Which json.dumps parameter is consulted exactly when the encoder meets a type it does not know?

scenarios.title: Paths that break on Windows
scenarios.situation: A script builds file paths with string concatenation and forward slashes. It works on Linux CI but fails on a teammate's Windows machine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the portable way to build paths?
evidence: path = base_dir + "/" + subdir + "/" + filename  # breaks on Windows
choices: pathlib.Path with the / operator — Path(base_dir) / subdir / filename uses the right separator per OS
os.path.join(base_dir, subdir, filename) — joins with the OS separator
Both pathlib and os.path.join are correct and portable — pick one and use it consistently
Hardcode backslashes and run everything under WSL
scenarios.why: Manual concatenation bakes in one platform's separator. Both os.path.join and pathlib handle separators, absolute/relative mixing, and normalization per OS. pathlib additionally offers readable method chaining (path.exists(), path.read_text()) and is the modern recommended API.
scenarios.hint: Which two stdlib options join path segments using the current operating system's separator?

scenarios.title: The regex that ate the page
scenarios.situation: A scraper extracts tag contents with <.*>, but on a line with two tags it returns everything from the first < to the last > as one match.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the pattern over-match, and how do you fix it?
choices: .* is greedy — it consumes as much as possible; use the non-greedy <.*?> or the precise <[^>]*>
findall returns overlapping matches by default — pass overlapped=False
Angle brackets need escaping — write \<.*\>
The pattern needs re.MULTILINE to handle multiple tags
scenarios.why: Greedy quantifiers match as much text as possible while still allowing the overall pattern to succeed, so <.*> spans from the first < to the last > on the line. The lazy .*? matches as little as possible, and [^>]* (any run of non-> characters) is even more precise and faster.
scenarios.hint: Does .* prefer to match more text or less text when both would satisfy the pattern?

scenarios.title: The meeting that moved an hour
scenarios.situation: Event times stored as naive datetimes shift by an hour for users after a daylight-saving transition, and subtracting two timestamps from different zones gives nonsense.
scenarios.prompt: What is the rule for correct datetime arithmetic across zones?
evidence:
start = datetime(2026, 3, 8, 1, 30)  # naive
end = datetime(2026, 3, 8, 3, 30)    # naive
(end - start).total_seconds() / 3600  # 2.0, but the wall clock skipped an hour
choices: Make datetimes timezone-aware (tzinfo=timezone.utc or ZoneInfo) — arithmetic on aware datetimes accounts for DST transitions
Store times as strings in ISO format and parse only for display
Always add one hour manually when the date falls in March or November
Use time.mktime to convert to epoch seconds before subtracting
scenarios.why: Naive datetimes carry no zone information, so subtraction assumes a fictional timeline with no DST gaps. Attaching a real tzinfo (via zoneinfo.ZoneInfo) makes the datetimes aware, and aware arithmetic follows actual elapsed time. Mixing naive and aware datetimes raises TypeError, which is the language telling you the comparison is meaningless.
scenarios.hint: What information is missing from a naive datetime that the arithmetic would need to handle a DST transition?

scenarios.title: Nested loops four deep
scenarios.situation: A test harness generates every combination of browser, OS, and locale with triple-nested for loops. Adding a fourth dimension means indenting everything again.
scenarios.prompt: Which itertools tool flattens the combination logic?
choices: itertools.product(browsers, oses, locales) — yields the Cartesian product as tuples in one loop
itertools.chain to concatenate the three lists into one sequence
itertools.groupby to cluster the dimensions before iterating
map() with a lambda over zip(browsers, oses, locales)
scenarios.why: itertools.product computes the Cartesian product of its inputs, replacing N nested loops with a single loop over tuples — and adding a dimension is just another argument. chain concatenates sequentially (not combinations), and zip pairs elements positionally instead of combining every possibility.
scenarios.hint: Which itertools function produces every combination of one item from each input iterable?

scenarios.title: Cleanup in the wrong clause
scenarios.situation: A teammate puts the success-path code in finally and the cleanup in else, and now cleanup is skipped whenever the operation raises.
scenarios.prompt: Which clause runs in which situation?
choices: The clauses are swapped: else runs only when no exception occurred (the success path), finally always runs (the cleanup)
else runs when an exception occurred — the code is correct as written
finally runs only on success — move use(result) into the try block
except catches everything — the else clause is unreachable
scenarios.why: The else clause of try/except runs only if the try block completed without raising — it is the success path. finally runs no matter what, making it the right home for cleanup like releasing locks. Swapping them inverts both guarantees.
scenarios.hint: Under what condition does the else clause execute — when the try raised, or when it did not?

scenarios.title: The traceback that lost its origin
scenarios.situation: A data loader catches a low-level parse error and raises a domain error, but the logs show only the new error — the original cause is invisible.
scenarios.prompt: How do you preserve the causal chain when translating exceptions?
choices: Use explicit chaining: raise LoadError(f"bad row {n}") from err — the traceback shows both exceptions
Log the ValueError and re-raise it unchanged instead of translating
Chain with the cause attribute: raise LoadError(...) .with_cause(err)
Exceptions cannot be chained in Python — catch at a higher level
scenarios.why: raise X from e sets __cause__, and the traceback prints 'The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception', preserving the full chain. (Implicit chaining via __context__ happens automatically, but explicit from documents intent and survives refactoring.)
scenarios.hint: Which three-word addition to a raise statement links it to the exception being handled?

scenarios.title: The service that would not stop
scenarios.situation: A worker loop wraps its body in a bare except: and logs errors. Operators find Ctrl-C no longer stops the process.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the bare except break KeyboardInterrupt, and what should it catch?
choices: Bare except catches BaseException, including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit — catch Exception instead
except: only catches SyntaxError — the real problem is the infinite loop
KeyboardInterrupt is raised asynchronously and cannot be caught at all
The loop needs a break in the except block to exit on Ctrl-C
scenarios.why: A bare except: catches every exception derived from BaseException — including KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl-C) and SystemExit — making the process unresponsive to normal shutdown signals. except Exception catches ordinary errors while letting control-flow exceptions propagate.
scenarios.hint: Which exception base class sits above both Exception and the interpreter's own control signals?

scenarios.title: print() in production
scenarios.situation: A service debugs with print() calls. In production the messages interleave, lack timestamps, and cannot be filtered by severity.
scenarios.prompt: What does the logging module provide that print() cannot?
evidence:
print(f"processing {order_id}")  # no timestamp, no level
print(f"ERROR: {e}")       # severity is just text
choices: Named loggers, severity levels, timestamps, and configurable handlers/filters — one basicConfig routes and formats everything
logging is faster than print because it buffers automatically
print cannot output to stderr — logging can
logging encrypts messages so they are safe in shared log aggregators
scenarios.why: The logging module gives every message a level (DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR/CRITICAL), a timestamp, and a source logger name, with handlers controlling where records go and filters controlling which pass. print() offers none of that — severity-by-text-convention breaks the moment anyone greps the logs.
scenarios.hint: What four things does every log record carry that a print() call does not?

scenarios.title: Reading the traceback backwards
scenarios.situation: A junior developer reads a traceback top-down, investigates the first frame, and wastes an hour — the actual bug is in their own code at the bottom.
scenarios.prompt: How do you read a Python traceback efficiently?
evidence:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "app.py", line 12, in <module>
    main()
  File "app.py", line 8, in main
    total = calc(items)
  File "lib.py", line 40, in calc
    return sum(x["price"] for x in items)
KeyError: 'price'
choices: Read bottom-up: the last line names the exception, and the innermost frame (closest to it) is where it was raised — then walk up to find your code
Read top-down: the first frame is always the bug location
Only the exception type matters — the frames are interpreter internals
Tracebacks list calls oldest-first, so the bug is in <module>
scenarios.why: 'Most recent call last' means the bottom frame is where the exception was raised. The last line gives the exception type and message (KeyError: 'price' — a dict missing a key), and scanning upward finds the first frame in your own code, which is where the fix belongs.
scenarios.hint: What does 'most recent call last' tell you about which frame raised the exception?

scenarios.title: The validation that vanished
scenarios.situation: Input validation written with assert() works in development, but invalid data sails through in production where Python runs with -O.
scenarios.prompt: Why is assert wrong for runtime validation, and what replaces it?
evidence:
def create_user(age):
    assert age >= 0, "age must be non-negative"
    ...
# production: python -O app.py  -> assertion silently skipped
choices: The -O flag strips assert statements entirely — validate with an explicit if and raise ValueError
assert only works in __init__ methods — move the check there
Assertions are for tests only and cannot carry messages — use print instead
-O disables exceptions globally, so no validation approach works under it
scenarios.why: assert is a debugging aid for internal invariants ('this should be impossible'), and Python's -O/optimize mode removes assert statements at compile time. Validation of external input must be unconditional code — if age < 0: raise ValueError(...) — which runs in every mode.
scenarios.hint: What does the -O flag do to assert statements, and should user-input validation depend on a debug aid?

Restart all components — Language Fundamentals issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately

domains.name: Start Here
domains.description: How to use this bootcamp, study strategy for Python interviews and certifications, and the Python lab environment guide.

scenarios.title: Navigating the bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You're new to Python and want to be interview-ready in 8 weeks, studying 6 hours a week.
scenarios.prompt: What's the right first two weeks?
choices: Jump to asyncio — it's the most modern topic
Do mock interviews first to benchmark
Read all lessons across 15 domains before writing code
Start-here (all 4 lessons), then fundamentals and data structures in order — the core language first; build the idiom notebook from day one
scenarios.why: Dependency order dominates Python learning: fundamentals and data structures underlie every interview question. Front-loading them builds the fluency everything else assumes.
scenarios.hint: Which domains do all the others assume?
evidence: start-here -> fundamentals -> data structures -> functions -> OOP

scenarios.title: Planning study time
scenarios.situation: You have 6 hours a week. You want interview skill, not just knowledge.
choices: All drills, no lessons
Cram everything in the last two weeks
2h lessons, 2h labs, 2h scenarios/code drills — interviews test writing code under pressure, and drills train exactly that; labs build the fluency
6h of lessons; coding later
scenarios.why: Interviews are performance: writing correct, idiomatic code live. An even split builds knowledge (lessons), fluency (labs), and performance (drills) together.
scenarios.hint: What do interviews actually test?
evidence: Lessons + labs + drills; performance is trained

scenarios.title: Using labs effectively
scenarios.situation: A lab asks you to write a decorator, but you've only read about them.
choices: Skip the lab — interviews matter more
Copy the example verbatim
Do the lab now — write it, break it (wrong scope, missing functools.wraps), fix it; the fix cycle is where decorator intuition forms
Re-read the lessons until confident
scenarios.why: Labs convert syntax into intuition, and deliberate breaking builds debugging skill. Interview code questions reward those who've seen code fail and fixed it.
scenarios.hint: When does the intuition actually form?
evidence: Write, break, fix — every example, every lab

scenarios.title: Mock interview strategy
scenarios.situation: First mock: you solve problems but slowly, with unidiomatic code. Three weeks left.
choices: Memorize solutions
Focus on problems you already solve well
Drill the weak patterns (the ones you fumbled) with timed reps, study idiomatic rewrites of your solutions, then re-mock — speed and idiom come from reps, not reading
Do a mock every day without review
scenarios.why: Mock analysis turns performance into a drill list: fumbled patterns get timed reps, unidiomatic solutions get rewritten. Daily mocks without review just rehearse the same slowness.
scenarios.hint: What does a fumbled pattern become?
evidence: Fumble -> timed drill -> idiomatic rewrite -> re-mock

domains.name: Mock Assessment
domains.description: Timed assessment shell — scenarios are drawn from all domains at runtime.

domains.name: Capstone: Task API Service
domains.description: Design and build a complete Python service: API, data layer, tests, packaging, and deployment.

scenarios.title: Capstone: model decision
scenarios.situation: Phase 1: you need to decide between dataclasses + manual SQL vs a full ORM for the task service.
choices: Raw SQL strings everywhere
No models — dicts throughout

Match to the project's needs: this service is small with simple queries — dataclasses + a thin repository keep it explicit and dependency-light; document the trade (ORM when relations/complexity grow)
Always use the heaviest ORM
scenarios.why: Tool choice follows complexity: the capstone's simple queries don't earn an ORM's abstraction cost, but the repository interface keeps the door open. The documented trade is the engineering judgment.
scenarios.hint: What would change the decision toward an ORM?
evidence: Complexity earns abstraction; document the trade

scenarios.title: Capstone: API error design
scenarios.situation: Phase 2: clients need to distinguish 'not found' from 'invalid input' from 'server error'.
choices: 500 for all errors
Different codes per endpoint inconsistently
Status codes as the language: 404 for missing tasks, 422 for validation errors, 500 only for real server failures — plus a consistent JSON error body with code and message; document every code
200 for everything, error in the body
scenarios.why: HTTP status codes are the API's contract: clients branch on them, monitoring alerts on 5xx rates. Consistent codes + structured bodies make the API predictable; 200-for-errors breaks every client assumption.
scenarios.hint: Why not 200 with an error field?
evidence: Status codes are the contract; bodies carry the detail

scenarios.title: Capstone: testing strategy
scenarios.situation: Phase 2: where do you put the testing effort — service layer, API layer, or both?
choices: Only API tests — they cover everything
Only unit tests — API is trivial
Manual testing with curl

Both, pyramid-style: many fast service-layer unit tests (business rules, no HTTP), fewer API tests (routes, status codes, validation) via test client — the service tests give speed, the API tests give contract confidence
scenarios.why: The test pyramid: unit tests are fast and precise (business rules), API tests verify the contract (status codes, shapes). API-only is slow and coarse; unit-only misses contract bugs; manual doesn't regress.
scenarios.hint: What does each layer catch that the other misses?
evidence: Pyramid: fast units for rules, API tests for contract

scenarios.title: Capstone: shipping checklist
scenarios.situation: Phase 3: the service works locally.
choices: Zip the source and email it
Deploy manually once
CI with the four gates (tests, coverage, lint, types), pinned dependencies, Docker image (slim, non-root, health check), README with setup and API docs — reproducible, verified, documented
It works on my machine — ship the laptop
scenarios.why: Shippable means reproducible and verified: CI proves it builds and passes elsewhere, Docker fixes the environment, docs let others run it. 'Works locally' is a demo, not a delivery.
scenarios.hint: What does CI prove that local runs don't?

scenarios.title: Capstone: the demo
scenarios.situation: Demo day: 5 minutes to show the task service.
choices: CI logs scrolling
Architecture diagrams only
Live API demo: create a task, list, complete it — the service doing its job; then the architecture slide (layers, tests, CI) — behavior first, structure second; stakeholders remember working software
Code walkthrough of every file
scenarios.why: Demos sell working software: the live flow proves it works, the architecture slide proves it's built right. Code tours and log scrolls are engineer-to-engineer content for a different meeting.
scenarios.hint: What do viewers remember from demos?

domains.name: Advanced Python
domains.description: Decorators, generators, context managers, metaclasses, and the data model — Python beyond the basics.

scenarios.title: Decorator with arguments
scenarios.situation: You need a @retry(times=3, delay=1) decorator for flaky API calls.
choices: Decorator factory: three levels — retry(times, delay) returns the decorator, which takes fn, which returns wrapper(*a, **k) with the retry loop; @wraps preserves metadata
Two levels — decorator takes times directly
A class with __init__ taking fn and times
Global variables for times/delay
scenarios.why: Parameterized decorators are factories: the outer call takes the parameters and returns the actual decorator. Two levels can't receive both the args and the function. @wraps keeps debugging sane.
scenarios.hint: How many nesting levels does a parameterized decorator need?

scenarios.title: Memory-efficient pipeline
scenarios.situation: Process a 50GB log file: filter errors, parse, aggregate counts — on a 4GB machine.
choices: Read all lines into a list first
Load into pandas
Split the file manually into chunks
Generator pipeline: (parse(l) for l in lines if is_error(l)) fed to a Counter — lazy, O(1) memory; materializing any stage blows the 4GB budget
scenarios.why: Generators compose lazily — each stage pulls from the previous, so only one line is in flight. Any materialization (list, DataFrame) needs the 50GB. The pipeline shape is the answer.
scenarios.hint: What makes the pipeline O(1) memory?

scenarios.title: Transaction safety
scenarios.situation: Database code must commit on success, roll back on exception — across 20 functions.
choices: Hope for no exceptions
@contextmanager transaction(): yield the connection; commit after yield, rollback on exception — with transaction(): replaces 20 try/except blocks with one pattern
try/except in each function
A base class with commit/rollback methods
scenarios.why: The context manager factors the acquire/release pattern once — every call site gets correctness by construction. Copy-pasted try/except drifts; the with-block can't.
scenarios.hint: What does the context manager guarantee?

scenarios.title: Making a class Pythonic
scenarios.situation: A Playlist class should support len(), for-loops, and 'in'.
choices: Implement __len__, __iter__, __contains__ delegating to the internal list — the container protocol; Python provides the syntax from the protocols
Add len(), iterate(), contains() methods
Subclass list
Document that users should access ._songs
scenarios.why: Protocols over methods: implementing the dunders makes built-in syntax work — len(p), for s in p, s in p. Custom method names don't integrate; subclassing list inherits unwanted behavior.
scenarios.hint: Which dunders form the container protocol?

scenarios.title: Type-based dispatch
scenarios.situation: A render() function handles str, list, dict, and custom types — growing monthly.
choices: functools.singledispatch: @singledispatch base + @render.register(type) per type — open for extension without modifying the dispatcher; no isinstance chain to rot
isinstance chain
Separate functions per type, caller chooses
A dict mapping types to functions
scenarios.why: singledispatch is the open/closed answer: new types register without touching existing code. isinstance chains grow linearly and rot; caller-chooses leaks the decision everywhere.
scenarios.hint: What principle does singledispatch serve?

scenarios.title: Expensive attribute
scenarios.situation: An object has an attribute costly to compute, used rarely.
choices: A method get_expensive() callers must remember
Global cache dict
Lazy proxy via __getattr__: compute on first access, cache the result — pay the cost only when used, transparent to callers
Compute in __init__ always
scenarios.why: Lazy loading defers cost to first use — __getattr__ intercepts the missing attribute, computes, caches. Eager __init__ pays always; manual methods leak the optimization into every caller.
scenarios.hint: When is the cost paid with lazy loading?
evidence: __getattr__ lazy proxy: compute once, on first access

scenarios.title: Combinatorial generation
scenarios.situation: Generate all 2-item combinations from a list for pair analysis.
choices: itertools.permutations (wrong — order matters there)
itertools.combinations(items, 2) — lazy, correct, readable; the stdlib answer for combinatorics
Nested for loops with index juggling
Recursive custom generator
scenarios.why: itertools.combinations is the exact tool: lazy, no index bugs, self-documenting. Nested loops reinvent it with off-by-one risk; permutations answers a different question (ordered pairs).
scenarios.hint: Combinations vs permutations — which and why?

domains.name: Concurrency and Async
domains.description: Threading, multiprocessing, asyncio, and choosing the right concurrency model.

scenarios.title: Choosing parallelism
scenarios.situation: You need to parallelize: (a) 1000 image thumbnails, (b) 1000 URL fetches.
choices: Multiprocessing for both
(a) multiprocessing — CPU-bound pixel work, GIL-bound in threads; (b) threading/asyncio — I/O-bound waiting, GIL released during waits
(a) threading, (b) multiprocessing
Threading for both
scenarios.why: Workload type decides: CPU-bound needs separate interpreters (processes); I/O-bound needs waiting overlap (threads/async). Swapped, thumbnails stay GIL-serialized and fetches pay pickling overhead.
scenarios.hint: What question determines threads vs processes?

scenarios.title: Thread pool sizing
scenarios.situation: Fetching 500 URLs with ThreadPoolExecutor.
choices: As many as CPU cores
Small multiple of expected concurrency (8-32) — threads wait on I/O, so more threads than CPUs helps, but thousands of threads waste memory; bound it and measure
1000 workers — one per URL
1 worker — safest
scenarios.why: I/O-bound threads: oversubscribe CPUs (waiting isn't computing) but bound the count — thread stacks cost memory, and context switching has limits. Measure throughput vs workers to find the knee.
scenarios.hint: Why more threads than CPUs for I/O work?
evidence: I/O threads: oversubscribe modestly, measure the knee

scenarios.title: Race condition
scenarios.situation: Two threads increment a shared counter; final counts are randomly low.
choices: Run threads sequentially
Use a global variable instead
Eliminate sharing (each thread counts locally, sum at the end) or guard with a lock — the read-modify-write isn't atomic; best fix is the design that doesn't share
Add time.sleep to desynchronize
scenarios.why: The increment isn't atomic: load-add-store interleaves. Locking serializes it; eliminating sharing removes the problem structurally. Sleep changes timing, not correctness; sequential defeats the purpose.
scenarios.hint: Why is increment not thread-safe?
evidence: Read-modify-write needs a lock — or no sharing

scenarios.title: Blocking in async
scenarios.situation: An async web handler calls a blocking database driver; under load, all requests stall.
choices: More event loops
Faster database
Synchronous handlers instead
Run the blocking call in a thread pool via loop.run_in_executor — the event loop stays free for other coroutines; or switch to an async driver
scenarios.why: One blocking call stalls the entire loop — every coroutine waits. run_in_executor moves the blocking work to a thread, keeping the loop responsive. The async model requires non-blocking I/O throughout.
scenarios.hint: What does one blocking call do to the loop?
evidence: Never block the loop — executor or async driver

scenarios.title: 10k connections
scenarios.situation: A gateway must hold 10,000 idle websocket connections with occasional messages.
choices: 10,000 threads
10,000 processes
Polling with cron
asyncio — 10k threads exhaust memory (stacks), 10k processes are absurd; one loop with 10k coroutines is exactly asyncio's design center
scenarios.why: Massive idle concurrency is asyncio's home turf: coroutines are kilobytes, threads are megabytes. Thread-per-connection dies at this scale; the event loop was built for C10k.
scenarios.hint: Why not threads at 10k connections?
evidence: C10k idle connections = asyncio's design center

scenarios.title: Backpressure
scenarios.situation: A fast producer outruns slow consumers; memory grows unboundedly.
choices: Bigger machine
Faster consumers (can't — they're I/O bound)
Unbounded queue with monitoring
Bounded queue (maxsize) — producers block when full, creating natural backpressure; the system self-throttles instead of OOMing
scenarios.why: Bounded queues convert memory risk into throughput shaping: the producer waits instead of buffering infinitely. Monitoring an unbounded queue observes the crash; bounding prevents it.
scenarios.hint: What does maxsize buy you?

scenarios.title: Graceful shutdown
scenarios.situation: Workers process queue items; deploys kill workers mid-item, losing work.
choices: Kill -9 faster
Smaller items
Duplicate every item
Shutdown protocol: stop accepting new items, drain the queue (workers finish current items), then exit — SIGTERM handler initiating the drain; in-flight work completes
scenarios.why: Graceful shutdown is a protocol: signal -> drain -> exit. In-flight items complete; queued items finish before the process dies. Hard kills trade deploy speed for lost work.
scenarios.hint: What are the phases of graceful shutdown?

domains.name: Testing and Quality
domains.description: pytest, fixtures, mocking, coverage, linting, and type checking for professional Python.

scenarios.title: Expensive setup
scenarios.situation: Each test needs a database with migrated schema — 2s setup per test, 200 tests.
choices: Session-scoped fixture for the schema (migrate once), function-scoped transaction rollback per test for isolation — speed from sharing, isolation from transactions
Function-scoped: migrate per test (400s suite)
Session-scoped with shared mutable data (test pollution)
No database — mock everything
scenarios.why: Two concerns, two scopes: schema setup is expensive and immutable (session), test data must be isolated (transaction rollback per test). Sharing mutable data across tests creates order-dependent failures.
scenarios.hint: How do you get both speed and isolation?

scenarios.title: What to mock
scenarios.situation: Testing checkout(): it calls charge_card() (external API), saves to DB, sends email.
choices: Mock checkout() itself
Mock at the seams: charge_card (external, slow, costs money) and send_email (side effect); use a real test database (or fake repository) for the save — mock I/O boundaries, not your logic
Mock everything including the DB save
Mock nothing — hit the real API
scenarios.why: Mock boundaries, not internals: external services are slow/costly/flaky (mock them); your own persistence logic is what you're testing (use a test DB). Mocking everything tests the mocks.
scenarios.hint: Where is the seam in this test?
evidence: Mock I/O boundaries; test your logic for real

scenarios.title: Case explosion
scenarios.situation: A validator needs 30 input cases tested.
choices: Test 3 representative cases
@pytest.mark.parametrize with the 30 (input, expected) pairs — one test function, 30 cases, each reported independently; adding case 31 is one tuple
30 separate test functions
One test with a for loop and asserts
scenarios.why: Parametrize is the case-table pattern: each case runs independently (one failure doesn't hide others), and the table documents the spec. Loops hide which case failed; 30 functions drown the file.
scenarios.hint: Why not a for loop with asserts?

scenarios.title: Coverage theater
scenarios.situation: Coverage is 95% but bugs keep shipping. Tests have few asserts.
choices: Delete the coverage gate
Coverage without assertions is theater — executed isn't tested; fix by asserting behavior (outputs, state changes, interactions), and consider mutation testing to verify the tests actually catch bugs
Push coverage to 100%
More tests with no asserts
scenarios.why: The metric became the target: lines execute, nothing is verified. Assert behavior and outcomes; mutation testing (does the test fail if the code is broken?) is the real quality check.
scenarios.hint: What does an assert-less test prove?
evidence: Assert behavior, not execution; mutation-test the suite

scenarios.title: CI quality gates
scenarios.situation: Setting up CI for a Python service.
choices: No gates — trust the developers
pytest (correctness) + coverage threshold (habit) + ruff (hygiene) + mypy (contracts) — four gates, each catching a different bug class, all blocking the merge
Tests only — the rest is noise
Lint only — tests are slow
scenarios.why: Each gate catches what the others miss: tests catch logic bugs, coverage enforces testing habit, ruff catches hygiene, mypy catches type errors. Together they're the automated code review.
scenarios.hint: What bug class does each gate catch?
evidence: Tests + coverage + lint + types, all blocking

scenarios.title: Slow integration tests
scenarios.situation: Integration tests take 10 minutes; developers stop running them.
choices: Run everything always (developers wait)
Only run tests in CI, never locally
Mark and separate: @pytest.mark.integration, unit suite runs in seconds on every change, integration runs in CI (and on demand) — fast feedback by default, full verification in the pipeline
Delete integration tests
scenarios.why: Feedback speed determines whether tests run: the unit suite must be seconds-fast for the red-green loop; integration moves to CI where minutes are acceptable. Deleting them loses the coverage; forcing waits loses the developers.
scenarios.hint: What determines whether tests get run?
evidence: Fast units locally, integration in CI

scenarios.title: mypy value
scenarios.situation: A teammate asks: 'we have tests, why add mypy?'
choices: mypy replaces tests
Only for large teams
Different bug classes: tests catch runtime behavior bugs, mypy catches type-contract bugs (wrong arg types, None where X expected) before runtime — and hints document the API contract for readers
No good reason — skip it
scenarios.why: Types and tests are complementary: mypy proves the contracts statically (cheap, instant), tests prove behavior dynamically. Hints also document — the signature is the first documentation readers see.
scenarios.hint: What does mypy catch that tests miss cheaply?

domains.name: Packaging and Deployment
domains.description: Packaging with pyproject, virtual environments, Docker, and CI/CD for Python projects.

scenarios.title: Dependency conflict
scenarios.situation: Two libraries need different versions of the same transitive dependency.
choices: Pin in the lock file with pip-compile, test the combination, and constrain the direct deps to the compatible range — reproducible resolution, verified by the test suite
Install both versions
Vendor one library's source
Ignore — it works today
scenarios.why: Lock files make the resolution explicit and reproducible; the test suite verifies the combination works. 'Works today' without pins breaks on the next fresh install.
scenarios.hint: What makes dependency resolution reproducible?
evidence: Lock file + compatible bounds + test verification

scenarios.title: Bloated image
scenarios.situation: The Python Docker image is 1.2GB; deploys are slow.
choices: Delete tests from the repo
Use a bigger registry
Slim base image, multi-stage build (compile in builder, ship artifacts), .dockerignore, --no-cache-dir, non-root user — each layer choice compounds; measure with dive
It's fine — storage is cheap
scenarios.why: Image size is deploy time and attack surface: slim bases, multi-stage builds, and ignored contexts each cut hundreds of MB. Measure per-layer to find the offenders.

scenarios.title: Flaky CI

scenarios.title: Closure trap
scenarios.situation: Stem: 'What does this print?' [lambda x: x + i for i in range(3)] applied to 10.
choices: Error
[12, 12, 12] — late binding: all lambdas capture the variable i, not its value; by call time i is 2 for all three. Fix: lambda x, i=i: x + i
scenarios.why: Closures capture variables, not values — the loop variable's final value (2) is what all three lambdas see. The default-arg trick (i=i) binds the current value. This is the most-asked Python gotcha.
scenarios.hint: Do closures capture variables or values?

scenarios.title: Mutable default
scenarios.situation: Stem: 'What happens when this is called twice?' def f(x=[]): x.append(1); return x.

Error on second call

scenarios.why: Default arguments evaluate once at function definition — the mutable default persists. The None-pattern is the standard fix. Recognize this on sight; it's asked constantly.

lessons.title: Language Fundamentals — Core concepts
concepts: Closures capture variables by reference, not values.
Late binding: binding the value at definition time — lambda i=i: print(i) — gives each callback its own copy.

Division semantics: floating-point division plus rounding discards the remainder: 100/3 rounds to 33 three times, totaling 99. divmod(100, 3) returns (33, 1), letting you distribute the leftover cent explicitly so the shares always sum to the original total.
String interning: cPython interns some string literals, which is why the check accidentally works in the REPL, but a string parsed from JSON is a distinct object with equal value.

example.walkthrough: The is operator tests whether two names point to the same object in memory. Value comparison with == is the correct test.

pitfalls: Common trap: string interning is disabled in production.
Common trap: list comprehensions share one lambda object.
Common trap: list multiplication shares one int object.
Common trap: range(5) yields the same object five times.

lessons.title: Data Structures — Core concepts
concepts: Idiomatic stdlib: the hand-rolled loop reimplements what the stdlib already provides, tested and optimized.
Memory efficiency: since the pipeline consumes rows exactly once, laziness cuts peak memory from O(n) to O(1) per row.

Dict keys: counter is a dict subclass built exactly for frequency counting; its constructor consumes an iterable and most_common(n) returns the n highest counts without a manual sort. Dict lookup hashes the key, and lists are mutable so Python makes them unhashable — a key whose hash could change would corrupt the table.

example.code:
ids = [7, 3, 7, 1, 3, 9]
unique = list(set(ids))  # order lost: [1, 3, 7, 9] or arbitrary
example.walkthrough: Sets are unordered by design, so converting through one discards the original sequence. Since Python 3.7 dicts preserve insertion order, dict.fromkeys(ids) keeps the first occurrence of each ID and drops later duplicates, and list() converts back.

pitfalls: Common trap: lists cannot be dict keys on 64-bit Python.
Common trap: dict keys must be strings.
Common trap: list(ids).remove duplicates with a nested loop checking index().
Common trap: read the file in binary mode to halve the memory footprint.

lessons.title: Functions & Modules — Core concepts
concepts: Function semantics: a transparent wrapper must accept everything the wrapped function accepts. *args captures positional arguments only; without **kwargs, any keyword argument raises TypeError.
*args/**kwargs: fix it by def wrapper(*args, **kwargs) with fn(*args, **kwargs).
Principle: python evaluates default argument expressions once, when the def statement runs.

example.walkthrough: The limit (default 1000) guards the C stack; each Python frame consumes C stack space, so raising the limit risks a hard segfault instead of a catchable error. An explicit list-based stack converts the traversal to iteration with heap-allocated memory, which scales to arbitrary depth.

pitfalls: Common trap: decorators cannot wrap functions with defaults.
Common trap: helper modules must be installed with pip before any script can import them.
Common trap: the wrapper must be defined with functools.partial, not a nested def.
Common trap: assign wrapper.__name__ = fn.__name__ manually at the end of the decorator.

lessons.title: OOP — Core concepts
concepts: Class vs instance attributes: attributes defined directly in the class body belong to the class object, and self.items.append mutates that single shared list rather than creating per-instance state. Attribute lookup walks the class's MRO — the C3 linearization shown by __mro__ — and uses the first match.

__init__: initializing self.items = [] inside __init__ gives every instance its own list. Defining __init__ in a subclass replaces the base version entirely; base-class initialization only happens if the subclass explicitly cooperates via super().__init__(...).
super(): cooperative mixins call super().save() so every mixin in the chain gets its turn.

example.walkthrough: Set membership hashes the object first and only calls __eq__ on hash collisions. When a class defines __eq__ without __hash__, Python sets __hash__ to None, making instances unhashable-by-value — they fall back to identity hashing, so equal SKUs land in different buckets. The rule: objects that compare equal must hash equal.

pitfalls: Common trap: python requires __init__ chaining via Shape.__init__(self, color) only, never super().
Common trap: color must be a class attribute.
Common trap: the last base class always wins.
Common trap: make balance private and add a set_balance method callers must use.

lessons.title: Stdlib & Files — Core concepts
concepts: File I/O: with open(...) as f: ties the file's lifetime to the block: __exit__ closes the handle whether the block completes, raises, or returns.
json module: the json module only handles dict, list, str, int, float, bool, and None.

pathlib: both os.path.join and pathlib handle separators, absolute/relative mixing, and normalization per OS. pathlib additionally offers readable method chaining (path.exists(), path.read_text()) and is the modern recommended API.

example.code:
payload = {"user": "amy", "at": datetime.now(timezone.utc)}
json.dumps(payload)  # TypeError: Object of type datetime is not JSON serializable
example.walkthrough: The json module only handles dict, list, str, int, float, bool, and None. Its default parameter is a function called for anything else — default=str converts datetimes via str(), while a custom function can emit isoformat() for precise round-tripping. pickle is not a substitute: it is Python-specific and unsafe on untrusted data.

pitfalls: Common trap: convert the payload with str(payload) and send that instead of JSON.
Common trap: use pickle instead of json.
Common trap: always add one hour manually when the date falls in March or November.
Common trap: store times as strings in ISO format and parse only for display.

lessons.title: Errors & Debugging — Core concepts
concepts: Exception chaining: a bare except: catches every exception derived from BaseException — including KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl-C) and SystemExit — making the process unresponsive to normal shutdown signals. except Exception catches ordinary errors while letting control-flow exceptions propagate.
raise from: validation of external input must be unconditional code — if age < 0: raise ValueError(...) — which runs in every mode.
Exception hierarchy: 'Most recent call last' means the bottom frame is where the exception was raised.

example.code:
print(f"processing {order_id}")  # no timestamp, no level
print(f"ERROR: {e}")       # severity is just text
example.walkthrough: The logging module gives every message a level (DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR/CRITICAL), a timestamp, and a source logger name, with handlers controlling where records go and filters controlling which pass. print() offers none of that — severity-by-text-convention breaks the moment anyone greps the logs.

pitfalls: Common trap: tracebacks list calls oldest-first, so the bug is in <module>.
Common trap: chain with the cause attribute: raise LoadError(...) .with_cause(err).
Common trap: the loop needs a break in the except block to exit on Ctrl-C.
Common trap: logging encrypts messages so they are safe in shared log aggregators.

lessons.title: Python — Core concepts
concepts: Lists, dicts, sets, and tuples are the working vocabulary: dicts and sets give average O(1) membership and lookup via hashing, lists give ordered O(1) indexing, and tuples are immutable sequences often used for fixed-shape records.

Functions are first-class: they can be passed around, returned, and closed over. A closure captures variables from the enclosing scope, which is why a loop variable referenced inside a lambda surprises people — it binds late, at call time.

Classes define behavior; instances hold state. Special (dunder) methods like __len__, __iter__, and __eq__ let your objects speak the language of the built-ins, and properties give you validated attribute access without breaking the attribute-access API.

The standard library covers most everyday needs: pathlib for paths, collections (Counter, defaultdict, deque), json, argparse for CLIs, logging instead of print, and unittest/pytest-style testing via the built-in unittest module.

Virtual environments isolate dependencies per project: `python3 -m venv .venv` creates one, activation puts its bin first on PATH, and pip then installs into the venv's site-packages instead of the system interpreter's.

Debugging beats guessing: read the traceback bottom-up (exception type, then the frame that raised it), reproduce minimally, and use pdb — `breakpoint()` drops you into an interactive shell at that exact line with the live state.

example.code:
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

counts = Counter()
for line in Path("access.log").read_text().splitlines():
    status = line.split()[8]          # 9th field: HTTP status
    counts[status] += 1               # missing keys start at 0

print(counts.most_common(5))
example.walkthrough: Counter is a dict subclass that defaults missing keys to 0, so counts[status] += 1 never raises KeyError. pathlib reads the whole file cleanly, and most_common(5) returns the top five codes as (code, count) pairs.

pitfalls: Common trap: using a mutable default argument (`def f(x=[])`) — the default is created once at def time and shared across calls.
Common trap: modifying a list while iterating over it — iterate over a copy (`for x in items[:]`) or build a new list.
Common trap: comparing with `is` instead of `==` — `is` checks identity, and small-int/string interning makes it pass sometimes and fail mysteriously other times.
Common trap: catching a bare `except:` — it swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit; catch the specific exception you expect.

lessons.title: Phase 1: Design and Data Layer
concepts: The capstone builds a task API service: tasks with titles, priorities, due dates, and status. Phase 1 designs the data model (dataclasses or ORM models), the storage layer, and the API contract.

Design decisions: data model first (what is a task?), storage interface (abstract the persistence — SQLite for the build, swappable later), and API shapes (request/response schemas). Decide deliberately, document briefly.
The storage abstraction: a TaskRepository protocol with save/get/list methods. Business logic depends on the protocol, not SQLite — testability and swappability by design.
Deliverable: models, repository interface + SQLite implementation, and tests for the data layer. Tested data layer before any API code — the foundation first.

class Task:

    title: str
    priority: int = 3
    due: date | None = None
    done: bool = False

lessons.title: Variables, Types, and Dynamic Typing
concepts: Python is dynamically typed: variables are names bound to objects, not typed boxes. x = 5 then x = 'hi' rebinds the name — the object carries the type, the name doesn't.
Core types: int (arbitrary precision — no overflow), float, str (immutable), bool, None. Know which are immutable (int, str, tuple) vs mutable (list, dict, set) — mutation bugs start here.
Type hints (x: int = 5) document intent; they don't enforce. mypy enforces statically. Professional code hints public interfaces; hints are documentation the tooling can check.
Identity vs equality: is compares object identity, == compares value. Use is only for None and singletons — 'if x is None', never 'if x == None'. Small-int caching makes 'is' on numbers a trap.

example.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a        # same object!
b.append(3)
print(a)     # [1, 2, 3] — aliasing, not copying
example.walkthrough: Assignment binds names to objects — b = a shares the list; mutate through either name.

pitfalls: Type hints expected to enforce at runtime.
