lessons.title: Control Flow: if, for, while, Comprehensions
concepts: for loops iterate iterables directly — 'for item in items', not index loops. range() for counts, enumerate() for index+value, zip() for parallel iteration. Index loops are the non-idiomatic smell.
Comprehensions: [x*2 for x in items if x > 0] — map+filter in one readable line. Keep them to one condition; nested double comprehensions become write-only code.
while for unknown iterations with a clear exit; break/continue for flow; for-else (else runs if no break) — rare but tested. Know it exists, use it sparingly.
Truthiness: empty collections, 0, None, '' are falsy. 'if items:' beats 'if len(items) > 0:' — idiomatic Python reads like English.

example.code:
squares = [x*x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
# [0, 4, 16, 36, 64] — even squares, one line
example.walkthrough: Comprehension with a filter: map (x*x) + filter (even) in a single expression.

lessons.try_it: Rewrite 3 loops as comprehensions

lessons.title: Strings: Formatting, Methods, and Encoding
concepts: f-strings are the modern format: f'Hello {name}, you are {age}!' — expressions allowed inside braces. % and .format() are legacy; know them for reading old code, write f-strings.
String methods: split/join (the pair — ','.join(list) not string concatenation in loops), strip, startswith, replace. Strings are immutable — methods return new strings.
Join beats +=: ''.join(parts) is O(n); s += part in a loop is O(n²). The performance trap in every interview's string-building question.
Encoding: str is Unicode; bytes is raw. Encode (str->bytes) for I/O, decode (bytes->str) on input. The boundary is explicit — UnicodeDecodeError means you guessed the encoding.

example.code:
words = ['a', 'b', 'c']
print(', '.join(words))  # 'a, b, c'
print(f'{len(words)} words')  # f-string
example.walkthrough: join/split are inverses; f-strings interpolate — the two string workhorses.

pitfalls: += in a loop for big joins.
lessons.try_it: Build a CSV line with join (not +=)

lessons.title: Numbers, Math, and Precision
concepts: int is arbitrary precision — 2**1000 just works. float is IEEE double — 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. Never use float for money; use Decimal for exact decimal arithmetic.
Division: / is true division (7/2 = 3.5), // is floor division (7//2 = 3), % is remainder, ** is power. divmod() gives both — the interview's 'quotient and remainder' answer.
Decimal for money: Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2') == Decimal('0.3'). Construct from strings, not floats — Decimal(0.1) inherits the float error.
Random: random module for simulations (seed for reproducibility); secrets for security (tokens, passwords). random is not cryptographic — the security interview trap.

example.code:
from decimal import Decimal
total = Decimal('19.99') + Decimal('5.00')
print(total)  # 24.99 exactly
example.walkthrough: Decimal from strings: exact money arithmetic, no float ghosts.

lessons.try_it: Compute a 3-item receipt with Decimal

lessons.title: Lists: Operations and Idioms
concepts: Lists are dynamic arrays: O(1) append/pop-from-end, O(n) insert/pop-from-front and membership tests. deque for queue behavior — popleft() is O(1).
Slicing: items[1:4], items[::-1] (reverse), items[:2] — slices copy. Slice assignment (items[1:3] = [...]) replaces spans. Know slice bounds never error (they clamp).
Sorting: sorted() returns new, .sort() sorts in place; key functions (key=len, key=lambda) customize. sorted(users, key=lambda u: u.age) — the interview pattern.
List as stack (append/pop) is natural; list as queue is the trap — collections.deque for FIFO. Unpacking: a, b, *rest = items — destructuring in one line.

example.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.append(4); q.popleft()  # O(1) both ends
example.walkthrough: deque is the queue; list is the stack — right structure, right complexity.

lessons.try_it: Implement a queue with deque, then with list; time both

lessons.title: Dictionaries: The Workhorse
concepts: Dicts are hash maps: O(1) get/set/delete by key. Keys must be hashable (immutable) — lists can't be keys, tuples can. Insertion-ordered since 3.7 — order is reliable.
Access patterns: d[key] (KeyError if missing), d.get(key, default), d.setdefault(key, []).defaultdict(list) for grouping — the 'group items by key' one-liner.
Dict comprehensions: {k: v*2 for k, v in d.items()}. Merging: {**a, **b} or a | b (3.9+). Counter for frequencies — the interview's 'most common' answer.
Never mutate a dict while iterating it — collect keys first or iterate a copy. RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration — the classic bug.

example.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
groups = defaultdict(list)
for name, dept in employees:
    groups[dept].append(name)
example.walkthrough: defaultdict groups without key-existence checks — the grouping idiom.

lessons.try_it: Group 20 items by category with defaultdict

lessons.title: Sets and Their Operations
concepts: Sets are unordered unique collections: O(1) membership, automatic dedup. Set operations — union (|), intersection (&), difference (-), symmetric difference (^) — answer 'in both'/'in either' questions directly.
Dedup: list(set(items)) removes duplicates (order lost); dict.fromkeys(items) dedups preserving order — the interview's follow-up.
Membership testing: 'x in my_set' is O(1) vs O(n) for lists. Hot-loop membership checks on lists are the performance bug; convert to set once.
frozenset: the immutable, hashable set — usable as dict keys and in other sets. Set of sets needs frozenset.

example.code:
seen = set()
unique = [x for x in items if not (x in seen or seen.add(x))]
# dedup preserving order, O(n)
example.walkthrough: The seen-set idiom: O(n) dedup with order — know it cold.

pitfalls: Mutable set as a dict key.
lessons.try_it: Find common/differing items between two lists with set ops

lessons.title: Tuples, NamedTuples, and Records
concepts: Tuples are immutable sequences: fixed structure, hashable, unpackable. Use for records (name, age), not for homogeneous collections (that's a list).
NamedTuple: tuple with named fields — Point(x=1, y=2), self-documenting, still a tuple (unpacks, hashes). dataclasses are the heavier alternative; NamedTuple is the light record.
Unpacking: x, y = point; first, *rest = items; a, b = b, a (swap). Multiple return values are tuple packing — 'return x, y' returns one tuple.
When tuple vs list vs NamedTuple vs dataclass: fixed heterogeneous record -> NamedTuple/dataclass; homogeneous sequence -> list; hashable key -> tuple/frozenset.

example.code:
from typing import NamedTuple
class Point(NamedTuple):
    x: float
    y: float
p = Point(1, 2); print(p.x, p[0])  # both work
example.walkthrough: NamedTuple: attribute access + tuple behavior — the light record type.

lessons.try_it: Model 3 record types with NamedTuple

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Structure
concepts: Decision framework: need O(1) lookup by key? dict. Unique membership? set. Ordered sequence? list. Fixed record? tuple/NamedTuple. FIFO? deque. Frequencies? Counter.
Complexity awareness: the interview asks 'how would you make this faster' — the answer is usually 'the right structure' (set for membership, dict for lookup, heapq for top-k).
Memory: __slots__ on classes with many instances; arrays for numeric bulk; generators instead of lists for pipelines. Structure choice includes resource profile.
Anti-patterns: list of pairs instead of dict (O(n) lookups), nested lists for records (unreadable), parallel lists instead of list of records (desync bugs).

example.code:
import heapq
top3 = heapq.nlargest(3, scores)  # O(n log k), not O(n log n)
example.walkthrough: nlargest for top-k: the right structure/algorithm beats full sort.

pitfalls: List scans where a set/dict fits.
lessons.try_it: Pick structures for 5 scenarios with justification

lessons.title: Defining Functions Well
concepts: Functions: single responsibility, verb names, return values over side effects. A function that both computes and prints is two functions — separate them.
Parameters: positional, keyword, defaults (immutable defaults only! def f(x=[]): is the classic bug — the list persists across calls), *args/**kwargs for flexibility.
Return early: guard clauses beat nested ifs. 'if not valid: return None' at the top flattens the function — readability is the feature.
Docstrings: one line for simple, Args/Returns for public. Type hints on signatures. The next reader (you, in 6 months) needs the contract.

example.walkthrough: Early return in the loop; None for 'not found' — the lookup pattern.

pitfalls: Deep nesting instead of guard clauses.
lessons.try_it: Fix a function with a mutable default bug

lessons.title: Scope, Closures, and Decorators Intro
concepts: LEGB rule: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in — name resolution order. nonlocal for enclosing-scope writes; global for module writes (avoid — return values instead).
Closures: inner functions capturing enclosing variables — the factory pattern. def make_adder(n): return lambda x: x + n. The captured n lives with the function.
Decorators: functions wrapping functions (@timer, @retry). def decorator(fn): @wraps(fn) def wrapper(...): ... — functools.wraps preserves the name/docstring. Without it, debugging lies.
Decorator with args: three nesting levels (decorator factory). Write the simple case fluently; recognize the factory pattern when reading.

example.walkthrough: The decorator skeleton: wraps preserves identity, *a/**k forwards everything.

pitfalls: global for what should be a return.
Late-binding closure in loops (the classic gotcha).
lessons.try_it: Write a retry decorator with @wraps

lessons.title: Lambdas, map/filter, and When Not To
concepts: lambda: anonymous one-expression functions — key=lambda u: u.age, sorted(key=...). One expression only; assignments and statements need def.
map/filter vs comprehensions: comprehensions are preferred ([f(x) for x in items] over map(f, items)) — more readable, Pythonic. map/filter survive mainly in functional-style code.
functools: partial (freeze arguments), reduce (fold — usually a loop is clearer), lru_cache (memoize pure functions — the performance freebie).
When not to: lambdas assigned to names (use def), complex logic in lambdas, map chains that a comprehension expresses better. Readability wins.

example.walkthrough: lru_cache memoizes the recursion — exponential to linear, one decorator.

pitfalls: reduce where a loop is clearer.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite 3 map/filter chains as comprehensions

lessons.title: Modules, Packages, and Imports
concepts: Modules are files; packages are directories with __init__.py (or namespace packages without). Import the specific name: from utils import parse — not import * (namespace pollution).
Absolute imports (from pkg.module import x) over relative for clarity — except intra-package relatives. Circular imports signal a design problem: extract the shared piece.
__name__ == '__main__' guard: importable module + runnable script. Code at top level runs on import — guard the side effects.
sys.path and the import system: Python searches installed packages then the script's directory. Virtual environments isolate this — the packaging domain builds on it.

example.code:
# utils.py
def parse(s): ...
# main.py
from utils import parse
if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(parse('input'))
example.walkthrough: Importable + runnable: the module works both ways with the guard.

pitfalls: from x import * in real code.
lessons.try_it: Structure a 3-module package cleanly

lessons.title: Arguments: Advanced Patterns
concepts: Keyword-only args (def f(*, strict=True)): callers must name them — API clarity. Positional-only (def f(x, /)): implementation detail. Use keyword-only for flags.
Unpacking calls: f(*args_list, **kwargs_dict) — forward arguments, build adapters. * in calls unpacks, ** unpacks mappings. The proxy/decorator pattern.
Default None pattern: def f(items=None): items = items or [] — the mutable-default fix. Sentinel objects for 'not provided' vs 'provided None'.
Type-hinted signatures: def process(items: list[str], strict: bool = False) -> list[str]: — the signature IS the documentation.

example.walkthrough: Keyword-only args: the call documents itself — no positional guessing.

lessons.try_it: Redesign 3 signatures with keyword-only args

lessons.title: Classes, Instances, and the Data Model
concepts: class defines the blueprint; __init__ initializes instance state. self is the instance — explicit, not magic. Attributes on self are per-instance; class attributes are shared.
The data model: __str__ (readable), __repr__ (unambiguous — the debugging one), __eq__/__hash__ (value semantics), __len__/__iter__ (container protocol). Implement the protocols your class promises.
__repr__ rule: eval-able when feasible, unambiguous always. Logging shows repr — a bad repr makes debugging blind.
Dataclasses: @dataclass auto-generates __init__/__repr__/__eq__ — the default for data-holding classes. Write manual classes only when behavior dominates.

example.walkthrough: Dataclass for the data, __str__ for the humans — the modern class default.

lessons.try_it: Convert 2 manual classes to dataclasses

lessons.title: Inheritance, Composition, and ABCs
concepts: Inheritance: 'is-a' relationships (Dog is an Animal). super().__init__() chains constructors — always call it. Method resolution order (MRO) handles diamonds; know it exists.
Composition over inheritance: 'has-a' beats 'is-a' for reuse (a Service has a Repository, not is a Repository). Inheritance for interface, composition for reuse — the design rule.
ABCs (Abstract Base Classes): @abstractmethod enforces the interface — subclasses must implement. The contract is compile-time-ish; violations fail at instantiation, not in production.
Mixins: small behavior classes (LoggingMixin) composed via multiple inheritance. Keep them stateless and narrow — mixins with state become MRO puzzles.

example.walkthrough: ABC: the interface contract — implementors must satisfy it.

lessons.try_it: Refactor an inheritance chain to composition

lessons.title: Properties, Classmethods, Staticmethods
concepts: @property: computed attributes with validation — obj.price reads like data, runs code. Setters validate: @price.setter rejects negatives. Encapsulation without getter/setter boilerplate.
@classmethod: operates on the class (cls) — alternative constructors (User.from_dict(d)). @staticmethod: namespaced utility, no cls/self — rare; module functions often better.
Descriptors (advanced): __get__/__set__ protocol behind property — know properties deeply; descriptors when building frameworks.
Private by convention: _internal (don't touch), __mangled (name-mangled for inheritance safety). Python trusts the programmer — conventions, not walls.

example.walkthrough: area reads as an attribute, computes on access — the property pattern.

pitfalls: staticmethod for what should be a function.
lessons.try_it: Add validated properties to 2 classes

lessons.title: Dunder Protocols in Practice
concepts: Container protocol: __len__, __iter__, __contains__ — your class works with len(), for loops, 'in'. Implement __iter__ via generators for lazy sequences.
Comparison: __eq__ + functools.total_ordering for the rest — define __eq__ and __lt__, get the family. Consistent ordering needs all-or-total_ordering.
Context manager protocol: __enter__/__exit__ — your class works with 'with'. Resource cleanup guaranteed — files, locks, transactions.
Callable: __call__ makes instances callable — function-like objects with state (counters, strategies). Know the protocol exists; use sparingly.

example.walkthrough: len() and for-loops just work — the container protocol in 4 lines.

pitfalls: Manual close() instead of context managers.
lessons.try_it: Make a class support len(), iteration, and 'with'

lessons.title: Design Patterns, Pythonically
concepts: Strategy: functions as strategies — pass the function, not a Strategy class hierarchy. First-class functions collapse half the GoF patterns.
Observer: callbacks or a simple event list — dict of event -> [handlers]. Libraries exist; the pattern is 10 lines when you need it.
Singleton: usually a module (imported once) — not a class with __new__ hacks. Borg pattern (shared __dict__) when instances must share state.
Factory: classmethods or plain functions returning instances — from_config() beats FactoryFactory. Python's dynamism makes most patterns lighter.

example.code:
# strategy as functions, not classes
def aggressive(prices): ...
def conservative(prices): ...
engine = Engine(strategy=aggressive)
example.walkthrough: Functions are strategies — the pattern without the boilerplate.

lessons.try_it: Implement strategy + observer Pythonically

lessons.title: Files and Paths with pathlib
concepts: pathlib is the modern path API: Path('data') / 'file.txt', .read_text(), .write_text(), .glob('*.csv'), .mkdir(parents=True). os.path is legacy — write pathlib.
Reading: .read_text() for small files; open() + iteration for large (streaming, not loading). Writing: .write_text() overwrites; append mode for logs.
Binary vs text: 'rb'/'wb' for bytes, encoding='utf-8' explicit on text. The encoding parameter prevents platform-dependent bugs.
Temp files: tempfile for scratch (auto-cleanup), and always clean up. Context managers for every open — leaked file handles are the silent bug.

example.code:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('data') / 'users.csv'
for line in p.open():
    process(line)  # streaming, constant memory
example.walkthrough: Iterate the open file — large files never fully load.

lessons.try_it: Rewrite 3 os.path snippets in pathlib

lessons.title: JSON, CSV, and Config
concepts: json: loads/dumps for strings, load/dump for files. Serializable types only — datetimes need a default handler or isoformat. Pretty-print with indent=2 for humans.
csv: DictReader/DictWriter with fieldnames — header-aware, robust. Never split(',') real CSVs (quoted commas break it) — the interview trap.
Config: tomllib (3.11+) for TOML, configparser for INI, environment variables for secrets (never config files for credentials). Layered: defaults < file < env < CLI.
Validation: parse then validate (pydantic/dataclasses) — 'parse, don't validate' is for types; for config, validate early and fail fast with clear messages.

example.code:
import csv
with open('users.csv') as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row['name'], row['email'])
example.walkthrough: DictReader: header-aware rows as dicts — never split(',').

lessons.try_it: Parse a CSV with quoted commas correctly

lessons.title: Datetime Done Right
concepts: datetime: naive (no tz) vs aware (with tzinfo) — never mix them (TypeError). Store UTC, display local. timezone.utc for creation, .astimezone() for display.
Parsing: fromisoformat() for ISO strings; strptime() with explicit formats otherwise. Formatting: strftime() or isoformat() — isoformat for storage interchange.
Arithmetic: timedelta for durations; dateutil for relative deltas (months). 'Next month' is not timedelta(days=30) — months vary.
The 3 rules: aware datetimes only, UTC internally, ISO format at boundaries. Every datetime bug violates one of these.

example.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
print(now.isoformat())  # '2026-10-10T...Z'-style, aware
example.walkthrough: UTC + aware + isoformat — the three rules in two lines.

lessons.try_it: Convert 3 naive datetimes to aware UTC

lessons.title: Subprocess and OS Interaction
concepts: subprocess.run(['ls', '-la'], capture_output=True, text=True) — the modern API. shell=True is the injection risk — pass arg lists, never format shell strings with user input.
Check results: .returncode, check=True to raise on failure, .stdout/.stderr captured. Silent failures (unchecked returncodes) are the bug class.
Environment: env={...} to control the child's environment; cwd= for working directory; timeout= to bound execution. Unbounded subprocesses hang pipelines.
When not subprocess: prefer stdlib (shutil, pathlib) over shelling out — fewer moving parts, no quoting bugs, cross-platform. Shell out only for tools without APIs.

example.code:
import subprocess
r = subprocess.run(['git', 'status', '--short'], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
print(r.stdout)
example.walkthrough: Arg list, captured output, check=True — the safe subprocess pattern.

pitfalls: Shelling out for what pathlib does.
lessons.try_it: Run 3 commands safely with run()

lessons.title: Logging Instead of Print
concepts: logging: getLogger(__name__), levels (DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR), handlers, formatters. Print is for humans; logging is for systems — severity, filtering, routing.
Configure once at the entry point (basicConfig or dictConfig); libraries only getLogger + log. Library configuring handlers is the anti-pattern.
Structured logging: log context (request_id, user) via adapters or structlog — greppable logs. 'ERROR: failed' without context is unfindable.
Levels discipline: DEBUG for diagnostics, INFO for milestones, WARNING for recoverable, ERROR for failures. Print-debugging in production code is the smell.

example.code:
import logging
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.info('order %s placed', order_id)  # lazy formatting
example.walkthrough: Module logger, lazy %s formatting — the logging idiom.

lessons.title: Exceptions: Raising and Handling
concepts: Raise specific exceptions: ValueError, KeyError, custom domain exceptions (class OrderError(Exception)). 'raise Exception(...)' is unhandled-able — specificity enables handling.
Handle what you can: try/except around the risky call, except SpecificError, else for the success path, finally for cleanup. Bare except: hides bugs — except Exception at boundaries, never bare.
Exception chaining: 'raise NewError(...) from original' preserves the cause. Lost tracebacks (bare raise in wrong place) make debugging archaeology.
EAFP (easier to ask forgiveness) vs LBYL (look before you leap): try/except KeyError beats 'if key in d' in concurrent code — the Pythonic default is EAFP.

example.walkthrough: EAFP lookup with a chained domain exception — the handling pattern.

lessons.title: Tracebacks: Reading and Debugging
concepts: Read tracebacks bottom-up: the last line is the error, the frames above show the call path. The file:line in YOUR code is the target — library frames are context.
Common tracebacks: NameError (typo/scope), TypeError (wrong type/args), AttributeError (wrong object), KeyError/IndexError (bad lookup), ImportError (path/env). Recognize each instantly.
pdb: breakpoint() drops you in — n(ext), s(tep), c(ontinue), p(rint), l(ist). Debug the running state, not the code in your head.
Reproduce first: the minimal failing case. 'Works on my machine' means the repro is incomplete — shrink it until it's deterministic.

example.walkthrough: breakpoint(): the debugger where you need it — no print archaeology.

lessons.title: Defensive Programming
concepts: Assertions for invariants: assert balance >= 0 — internal contracts, not user validation. -O strips them; never assert on user input.
Validation at boundaries: validate inputs at API edges (pydantic, manual checks), trust internals. The boundary is where garbage enters — guard it.
Fail fast: detect errors at the earliest point with the clearest message. Silent wrong results beat loud crashes in damage — crashing is the kindness.
Invariants documented: 'this list is always sorted' as a comment + assert. The next modifier knows the contract — or the assert tells them.

example.walkthrough: Assert the invariant, raise on the business rule — two different tools.

lessons.title: Testing Your Error Paths
concepts: Error paths need tests: pytest.raises(ValueError) for the raise, and tests for the except branches. Untested except blocks are where bugs hide — coverage should include them.
pytest.raises as context manager: with pytest.raises(InsufficientFunds): withdraw(10, 20). Match messages when the message is the contract.
Exception testing checklist: each custom exception raised somewhere is asserted somewhere; each except branch has a triggering test; boundary validation tested with bad inputs.
Mutation mindset: 'if I delete this except, does a test fail?' If not, the handler is untested. Coverage of the sad paths is the quality signal.

example.code:
import pytest
def test_overdraft():
    with pytest.raises(InsufficientFunds):
        withdraw(10, 20)
example.walkthrough: pytest.raises: the error-path test in three lines.

lessons.title: Debugging Strategy
concepts: Strategy: reproduce -> isolate (bisect the code) -> hypothesize -> test the hypothesis -> fix -> regression-test. Random changes are not debugging — the loop is.
Bisect: comment out half, does it still fail? Binary search the bug's location. Faster than reading 500 lines hoping the bug glows.
Rubber-duck: explain the code aloud — the bug surfaces when the explanation contradicts the code. The hypothesis must predict: 'if X, then changing Y fixes it'.
Regression test: every fixed bug gets a test that fails without the fix. The bug stays fixed because the test guards it — debugging without regression tests is temporary.

example.code:
# bisect: does it fail with half the pipeline?
# hypothesis: 'the sort key is None for missing ages'
# test: print the key for the failing record
# fix + regression test
example.walkthrough: The loop: reproduce, isolate, hypothesize, fix, guard.

pitfalls: No regression test for the fix.

lessons.title: Decorators Deep Dive
concepts: Decorators wrap functions: @retry, @cache, @authenticated. The pattern: decorator(fn) returns wrapper; wrapper calls fn with added behavior. functools.wraps preserves metadata.
Decorators with arguments: @retry(times=3) is a decorator FACTORY — three levels: factory(args) -> decorator(fn) -> wrapper(*a, **k). Read inside-out.
Class decorators and method decorators: same mechanism, different targets. @dataclass IS a class decorator — the most-used one in Python.
Order matters: @a @b def f applies b first, then a — bottom-up. Stacked decorators compose; the bottom one is closest to the function.

example.walkthrough: Decorator factory: three levels — factory takes args, decorator takes fn, wrapper takes call args.

pitfalls: Decorator args confused with function args.
Wrong mental order of stacked decorators.

lessons.title: Generators and Iterators
concepts: Generators: functions with yield — lazy sequences, O(1) memory. for x in gen() pulls values on demand. Infinite sequences become possible: while True: yield ....
Generator expressions: (x*2 for x in items) — lazy comprehension. Pipelines: (parse(l) for l in lines if valid(l)) — compose lazily, materialize at the end.
yield from delegates to sub-generators — flatten nested iteration. send()/throw() make coroutines (advanced) — know they exist; async/await superseded most uses.
Iterator protocol: __iter__ + __next__ — for loops consume iterators. Generators ARE iterators. One-shot: generators exhaust — re-iterating gives nothing (the classic bug).

example.walkthrough: Lazy line pipeline: memory stays flat regardless of file size.

lessons.title: Context Managers
concepts: with guarantees cleanup: files, locks, transactions, timers. __enter__/__exit__ protocol — __exit__ runs even on exceptions. Resource safety by construction.
@contextmanager: turn a generator into a context manager — yield separates setup from teardown. The 5-line pattern replacing a 20-line class.
Multiple managers: with a() as x, b() as y: — nested acquisition, reverse-order release. ExitStack for dynamic numbers of managers.
Write context managers for: timing blocks, temporary directory changes, database transactions (commit/rollback). The pattern generalizes to any paired acquire/release.

example.walkthrough: Generator-based context manager: code before yield sets up, after cleans up.

lessons.title: The Data Model: Dunders That Matter
concepts: Python's data model is protocols: __len__, __iter__, __contains__, __enter__/__exit__, __call__, __eq__/__hash__, __getattr__. Implement protocols, get syntax for free.
__getattr__ vs __getattribute__: the former is the fallback (missing attrs), the latter intercepts everything (easy infinite recursion). Proxies use __getattr__.
__slots__: no __dict__ per instance — memory savings for millions of instances. Trade: no dynamic attributes. Measure before optimizing.
Metaclasses (brief): classes of classes — __new__/__init__ on the metaclass customize class creation. Rarely needed; recognize when reading frameworks (ORMs, ABCMeta).

example.walkthrough: Lazy proxy via __getattr__: loads on first attribute access.

pitfalls: Metaclasses for what a decorator does.

lessons.title: Functional Tools: itertools and functools
concepts: itertools: infinite iterators (count, cycle), combinatorics (product, permutations, combinations), grouping (groupby — needs sorted input!). The lazy algorithm toolkit.
functools: partial (argument freezing), reduce (fold), lru_cache (memoization), total_ordering, singledispatch (type-based dispatch — polymorphism without classes).
singledispatch: @dispatch def process(x: int)... — function overloading by type. Clean alternative to isinstance chains.
operator module: itemgetter/attrgetter/methodcaller as key functions — sorted(users, key=attrgetter('age')). Faster and cleaner than lambdas.

example.walkthrough: Type-dispatched rendering — no isinstance chain.

lessons.title: Descriptors and Properties Internals
concepts: Descriptors: objects with __get__/__set__/__delete__ — property, classmethod, staticmethod ARE descriptors. Understanding them explains attribute access.
Custom descriptor: validated attribute type — class Positive: def __set__(self, obj, v): if v <= 0: raise ValueError. Reusable validation across classes.
When descriptors over properties: reuse across many attributes/classes. One-off validation -> @property; repeated -> descriptor. The reuse threshold decides.
Interview angle: 'how does @property work' — it's a descriptor installed as a class attribute. Knowing the mechanism beats reciting the usage.

example.walkthrough: Validated descriptor: reusable positive-number enforcement.

lessons.try_it: Build a typed-attribute descriptor

lessons.title: The GIL and What It Means
concepts: The GIL (Global Interpreter Lock): one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. CPU-bound threads don't parallelize in CPython — threads help I/O-bound work (waiting releases the GIL).
CPU-bound -> multiprocessing (separate interpreters, no shared GIL) or C extensions (numpy releases the GIL). I/O-bound -> threading or asyncio. The workload decides, mechanically.
GIL workarounds: multiprocessing for CPU, asyncio for massive I/O concurrency, Cython/C for hot loops. Don't fight the GIL — route around it by workload type.
Interview answer: 'threads for I/O, processes for CPU' — then the nuance (GIL, pickling costs, shared state). The one-liner plus the why.

example.code:
import time
# I/O-bound: threads win (waiting releases GIL)
# CPU-bound: threads DON'T speed up — use multiprocessing
example.walkthrough: The rule in one comment: workload type selects the tool.

pitfalls: Ignoring the GIL in design discussions.
lessons.try_it: Classify 6 workloads: threads vs processes vs async

lessons.title: Threading Done Right
concepts: threading.Thread for I/O-bound parallelism: network requests, file I/O. The GIL releases during I/O waits — threads genuinely overlap waiting.
ThreadPoolExecutor: submit tasks, get futures — the modern API. with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as ex: results = ex.map(fetch, urls). No manual thread management.
Shared state: locks (threading.Lock) for mutations, queues (queue.Queue) for communication. Prefer queues over shared mutable state — message passing beats locking.
Race conditions: the bug class — two threads mutating shared state. Reproduce with stress loops; fix with locks or (better) eliminate sharing. Daemon threads die with the program.

example.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as ex:
    pages = list(ex.map(fetch, urls))
example.walkthrough: Thread pool map: 8 concurrent fetches, results in order — the I/O pattern.

lessons.try_it: Fetch 20 URLs concurrently with a pool

lessons.title: Multiprocessing
concepts: multiprocessing: separate processes, separate GILs — true CPU parallelism. ProcessPoolExecutor mirrors the thread API: ex.map(compute, data).
Costs: process startup, data pickling between processes, no shared memory by default (use Value/Array/Manager sparingly — sharing reintroduces coordination costs).
Chunksize matters: many tiny tasks -> pickling overhead dominates; batch into chunks. ex.map(f, data, chunksize=100) for fine-grained work.
if __name__ == '__main__' guard REQUIRED on Windows/macOS (spawn) — unguarded code re-executes in children infinitely. The classic multiprocessing bug.

example.code:
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
    results = list(ex.map(expensive_compute, data, chunksize=50))
example.walkthrough: Process pool for CPU work: same API as threads, real parallelism.

pitfalls: No __main__ guard — fork bombs on spawn platforms.
lessons.try_it: Parallelize a CPU-bound loop; measure speedup

lessons.title: Asyncio Fundamentals
concepts: asyncio: single-threaded concurrency via event loop — coroutines (async def) yield control at await points. Thousands of concurrent I/O operations, one thread.
async def fetch(): ... await get(url) — await suspends THIS coroutine until the I/O completes; the loop runs others meanwhile. No threads, no GIL issues, no race conditions on shared state (mostly).
asyncio.gather(*coros) runs coroutines concurrently; asyncio.create_task() schedules background work. gather is the 'fetch all URLs' primitive.

When async: massive I/O concurrency (10k connections), async libraries exist (aiohttp, asyncpg). When not: CPU-bound (still GIL-bound), or sync libraries only — don't mix blocking calls in async code.

example.code:
import asyncio
async def main():
    pages = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(u) for u in urls))
asyncio.run(main())
example.walkthrough: gather: N concurrent fetches, one thread — the async workhorse.

pitfalls: Blocking calls inside async def (kills the loop).
lessons.try_it: Fetch 50 URLs with asyncio + aiohttp

lessons.title: Choosing the Concurrency Model
concepts: Decision tree: CPU-bound? -> multiprocessing. I/O-bound, moderate concurrency? -> threading. I/O-bound, massive concurrency? -> asyncio. Simple script? -> sequential (don't parallelize unnecessarily).
Hybrid: asyncio event loop + run_in_executor for blocking/CPU bits — async main with thread/process pools for the exceptions. Real systems mix models deliberately.
Complexity costs: threads (races), processes (pickling/IPC), async (function coloring — async infects callers). Each model has a tax; pay it only when the workload demands.
Interview framing: state the workload, pick the model, name the trade-off. 'I/O-bound with 10k connections -> asyncio; the trade-off is async-only libraries.'

example.code:
# decision as code comments
# 100 HTTP calls -> ThreadPoolExecutor (simple) or asyncio (scale)
# video encoding -> ProcessPoolExecutor
# 10k websockets -> asyncio
example.walkthrough: The decision tree as comments — workload in, model out.

lessons.try_it: Choose models for 5 architectures with rationale

lessons.title: Queues, Locks, and Coordination
concepts: Queues decouple producers/consumers: asyncio.Queue / queue.Queue / multiprocessing.Queue per model. Workers pull tasks; backpressure via maxsize — bounded queues prevent memory blowup.
Locks and semaphores: asyncio.Lock for async critical sections, Semaphore(10) to bound concurrency ('at most 10 concurrent fetches' — the rate-limit pattern).
Events and conditions: coordinate startup/shutdown — workers wait on an event, the main thread sets it. Clean shutdown beats daemon-kill.
Deadlock awareness: lock ordering (always acquire in the same order), timeouts on acquires, prefer lock-free designs (queues, immutable messages).

example.code:
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)
async def bounded_fetch(url):
    async with sem:
        return await fetch(url)
example.walkthrough: Semaphore bounds concurrency — 10 at a time, no more.

lessons.title: pytest Fundamentals
concepts: pytest: test functions (test_*.py, test_* functions), assert with plain asserts — pytest rewrites them for rich failure output. No boilerplate classes needed.
Fixtures: @pytest.fixture for setup — database connections, test clients, sample data. scope='module' for expensive setup; autouse sparingly.
Parametrize: @pytest.mark.parametrize('a,b,expected', [...]) — one test, many cases. The table-driven test — more cases, same code.
Running: pytest -x (stop on first failure), -k pattern (select), --lf (last failed), -v. The flags you'll use daily.

example.walkthrough: Parametrized: 3 cases, one test function — the table-driven pattern.

pitfalls: One assert per test dogma (group related).
lessons.try_it: Parametrize 5 cases for a function

lessons.title: Fixtures and Test Organization
concepts: Fixture scopes: function (default, isolated), module/class (shared expensive setup), session (DB container). Wider scope = faster but shared state — prefer narrow.
conftest.py: shared fixtures per directory — the test infrastructure. tmp_path fixture for file tests (auto-cleanup). monkeypatch for env vars and small patches.
Test layout: tests/ mirroring src/, one test file per module. Integration tests marked (@pytest.mark.integration) and separated — unit suite stays fast.
Fixture composition: fixtures requesting fixtures — build layered setup (db -> user -> order). Explicit dependencies beat hidden globals.

example.walkthrough: Composed fixtures: user needs db — declared as a parameter.

pitfalls: Session fixtures with mutable shared state.
lessons.try_it: Organize fixtures for a 3-layer app

lessons.title: Mocking and Test Doubles
concepts: unittest.mock: Mock() for collaborators, patch() to replace (patch('module.Class')), MagicMock for magic methods. Patch WHERE it's looked up, not where it's defined — the classic gotcha.
What to mock: I/O boundaries (HTTP, DB, filesystem, time) — not your own logic. Mocking internals makes tests mirror implementation; mock at the seam.
Fake vs mock: fakes are working implementations (in-memory repository); mocks verify interactions. Prefer fakes for state, mocks for 'was it called'.
Don't mock what you don't own (wrap external APIs in adapters, mock the adapter). Over-mocking creates tautological tests — testing the mock, not the code.

example.code:
from unittest.mock import patch
def test_notify():
    with patch('billing.send_email') as mock_send:
        checkout(user)
        mock_send.assert_called_once()
example.walkthrough: Patch at the lookup point; assert the interaction — the mock pattern.

pitfalls: Patching where defined, not looked up.
lessons.try_it: Write adapter + mock for an HTTP call

lessons.title: Coverage and Quality Gates
concepts: Coverage: pytest --cov=src --cov-fail-under=90 — measures executed lines. 90%+ for business logic; 100% is aspirational. Coverage of error paths matters most.
Coverage lies: executed != tested (assert-less tests 'cover'). Branch coverage (--cov-branch) is stricter. Mutation testing (mutmut) is the real check — rarely run, good to know.
Quality gates in CI: tests pass, coverage threshold, ruff clean, mypy clean. All four, every push. Gates automate discipline.
What not to chase: coverage of trivial code (getters), or gaming the number (pragma no cover on real logic). The gate serves quality; the number serves the gate.

example.code: pytest --cov=src --cov-branch --cov-fail-under=90 --cov-report=term-missing
example.walkthrough: Coverage with missing-line report — see exactly what's untested.

pitfalls: pragma no cover on real logic.
lessons.try_it: Get a module to 90% with meaningful tests

lessons.title: Linting with Ruff and Formatting
concepts: Ruff: the fast linter — pyflakes + pycodestyle + more, configured in pyproject.toml. ruff check . and ruff format . — lint and format in one tool.
Rule sets: enable E (errors), F (pyflakes), I (isort), UP (pyupgrade), B (bugbear). Start strict; disable per-line with # noqa: F841 and a reason — not file-wide.
Formatting: ruff format (black-compatible) — no style debates, the tool decides. Format on save in the editor; CI checks formatting.
Pre-commit: run ruff + format + mypy on commit — issues caught before push. The 2-minute setup that prevents 200 CI failures.

example.code: ruff check . && ruff format --check . && echo CLEAN
example.walkthrough: Lint + format check — the CI gate locally.

pitfalls: Style debates instead of a formatter.
No pre-commit — CI as the linter.
lessons.try_it: Configure ruff strict for a project

lessons.title: Type Checking with mypy
concepts: mypy: static type checking from hints — catches wrong-arg-type bugs before runtime. mypy src/ with strict = True for new code; gradual for legacy.
Hint the boundaries: public function signatures fully hinted; internals inferred. -> ReturnType always on public functions — the contract.
Common types: Optional[X], Union, list[str], dict[str, int], Callable, Protocol (structural typing — 'has these methods'). Protocol over ABC for flexibility.
Strictness ramp: start with basic mypy, enable strict incrementally (disallow_untyped_defs first). Legacy codebases go gradual — new code goes strict.

example.code: mypy --strict src/ 2>&1 | head -20
example.walkthrough: Strict mypy — the full check on new code.

pitfalls: Strict on day one for legacy code.
lessons.try_it: Add hints until mypy --strict passes on a module

lessons.title: pyproject.toml and Packaging
concepts: pyproject.toml: the modern packaging config — [project] metadata (name, version, dependencies), [build-system], [tool.ruff], [tool.pytest]. One file, everything declared.
Dependencies: declare direct deps with bounds (requests>=2.28,<3); pin transitives in requirements.lock or via pip-tools. Bounds for libraries, pins for apps.
Entry points: [project.scripts] mycli = 'pkg.cli:main' — pip install creates the command. The professional CLI distribution.
Build: python -m build creates sdist + wheel. Version from git tags (hatch-vcs) — single source of truth, no manual version bumps.

example.code:
[project]
name = 'taskapi'
version = '0.1.0'
dependencies = ['fastapi>=0.100', 'pydantic>=2.0']
[project.scripts]
taskapi = 'taskapi.cli:main'
example.walkthrough: Project metadata + CLI entry point — the packaging essentials.

lessons.title: Virtual Environments Done Right
concepts: venv per project: python3 -m venv .venv — isolated packages, reproducible. Activate (.venv/bin/activate) or run .venv/bin/python directly. Never sudo pip.
pip-tools: requirements.in (direct deps) -> pip-compile -> requirements.txt (pinned transitives). Reproducible installs; dependabot-style updates via recompile.
pipx for CLI tools (black, ruff as apps): isolated app environments, global commands. Tools via pipx, project deps via venv — separate concerns.
Docker + venv: venv inside the image is optional (the image IS the isolation) — but harmless and explicit. Multi-stage builds keep images slim.

example.code: python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e '.[dev]' && .venv/bin/pytest
example.walkthrough: Venv + editable install + tests — the dev loop in one line.

lessons.try_it: Set up pip-tools workflow for a project

lessons.title: Docker for Python Services
concepts: Dockerfile: slim base (python:3.12-slim), copy requirements first (layer cache), install, copy code, non-root USER, HEALTHCHECK, CMD. Order matters for build speed.
Non-root: RUN useradd app && USER app — containers shouldn't run as root. HEALTHCHECK hits /health — orchestrators restart unhealthy containers.
.dockerignore: .venv, __pycache__, .git, tests (maybe) — small contexts build fast. Context size is build time.
Multi-stage: builder (compile deps) -> runtime (slim + artifacts). Compiled extensions without build tools in prod.

example.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY src/ src/
RUN useradd -m app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health || exit 1
CMD ['python', '-m', 'taskapi']
example.walkthrough: Layer order (deps before code), non-root, healthcheck — the production Dockerfile.

lessons.try_it: Write a production Dockerfile for the capstone

lessons.title: CI/CD Pipelines
concepts: CI pipeline: checkout -> setup Python -> install deps -> ruff -> mypy -> pytest with coverage -> build package -> (Docker build). Every push, every PR — the quality gates automated.
Caching: cache pip downloads and venvs between runs — minutes saved per build. Matrix: test across Python versions (3.10, 3.11, 3.12) for libraries.
CD: tag -> build -> push image (immutable tags, not latest) -> deploy to staging -> smoke tests -> production. The pipeline is the deployment runbook.
Secrets in CI: never in code — CI secret stores, injected as env vars. The pipeline handles credentials; the repo never sees them.

example.code:
jobs:
  test:
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
      - run: pip install -e '.[dev]'
      - run: ruff check . && mypy src/ && pytest --cov-fail-under=90
example.walkthrough: The four gates in CI: lint, types, tests, coverage.

lessons.try_it: Write a CI workflow with all four gates

lessons.title: Dependency Management at Scale
concepts: Lock files for apps: pip-compile or poetry lock — every transitive dep pinned, reproducible installs. Libraries: bounded ranges (flexible for consumers).
Vulnerability scanning: pip-audit in CI — known CVEs in dependencies fail the build. Renovate/Dependabot PRs keep deps fresh — review and merge weekly.
Private indexes: extra-index-url for internal packages; authenticate via keyring/CI secrets, never hardcoded. Namespace your internal packages clearly.
Upgrade discipline: minor/patch promptly, majors deliberately (changelog + test suite). Pinned != frozen forever — stale pins accumulate CVEs.

example.code: pip-audit --strict && echo NO-KNOWN-CVES
example.walkthrough: Audit dependencies in CI — CVEs fail the build.

lessons.title: Twelve-Factor for Python Apps
concepts: 12-factor: config in env vars, stateless processes, backing services as attached resources, logs as event streams, disposability (fast startup/shutdown). The deployment checklist.
Config: pydantic-settings or environs — typed env config with defaults and validation. One settings object; no os.environ scattered through code.
Logs to stdout (the platform aggregates); metrics via prometheus_client; health endpoints (/health, /ready). Observable by default.
Graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM — finish in-flight requests, close connections. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL; the app should exit cleanly in the grace period.

example.code:
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings
class Settings(BaseSettings):
    db_url: str = 'sqlite:///app.db'
    debug: bool = False
settings = Settings()  # reads env automatically
example.walkthrough: Typed settings from env — config as code, validated at startup.

lessons.title: Interview Format and Question Types
concepts: Python interviews: live coding (write working code), code reading ('what does this print'), design ('how would you structure'), and trivia (rare, but exists). Prepare for all four — most candidates only drill coding.
Live coding rubric: correctness first, then clarity, then idiom, then complexity. Narrate your thinking — interviewers score the process, not just the result. Silent brilliance looks like luck.
Code-reading drills: trace tricky snippets (closures in loops, mutable defaults, generator exhaustion) by hand. The 'what does this print' questions test the mental model, not memory.
Time management: 45 minutes, 2-3 problems. Don't perfect problem 1 while problem 3 sits blank — working solutions to all beats perfect solutions to some.

example.code:
# drill: what does this print?
funcs = [lambda x: x + i for i in range(3)]
print([f(10) for f in funcs])  # [12, 12, 12] — late binding!
example.walkthrough: Late binding: all lambdas see i=2 — the closure trap in one line.

lessons.try_it: Trace 10 tricky snippets by hand

lessons.title: High-Frequency Idioms
concepts: The idiom checklist: comprehensions, unpacking, with-blocks, enumerate/zip, defaultdict/Counter, join, f-strings, any/all, sorted with key. Interview code should use them naturally.
any/all: any(x > 0 for x in items) — short-circuits, readable. 'Check if any/all satisfy' is any/all, not a loop with a flag.
Unpacking: a, *rest = items; x, y = y, x (swap); def f(a, *args, **kwargs). Destructuring everywhere — the fluent Python look.
Drill: take 10 loop-based solutions and rewrite idiomatically. The rewrite practice is what makes idioms automatic under pressure.

example.code:
# loop version vs idiom
found = False
for x in items:
    if x > 0: found = True; break
# idiom:
found = any(x > 0 for x in items)
example.walkthrough: any() replaces the flag loop — shorter, clearer, short-circuits.

lessons.try_it: Rewrite 10 loops idiomatically

lessons.title: Data Structure Choices Under Pressure
concepts: The interview's favorite follow-up: 'how would you make this faster?' — the answer is almost always the right structure: set for membership, dict for lookup, heapq for top-k, deque for queues.
Complexity statements: say them aloud — 'dict lookup is O(1), so the whole thing is O(n)'. Interviewers score complexity analysis explicitly.
Trade-off articulation: 'Counter uses O(k) extra memory for O(n) time' — state both sides. The senior answer names the trade, not just the speedup.
Practice: for 20 problems, state the naive structure, the better structure, and both complexities. The pattern becomes reflex.

example.walkthrough: The seen-set: O(n) duplicates — the structure IS the optimization.

lessons.try_it: State structures + complexities for 20 problems

lessons.title: OOP and Design Questions
concepts: OOP interview questions: 'design a deck of cards', 'implement LRU cache', 'model a parking lot'. Approach: clarify requirements, identify classes, define interfaces, then code the core.
LRU cache: the classic — OrderedDict or dict + doubly-linked list. Know the OrderedDict one-liner AND the manual version; interviewers ask for both levels.
Design principles to voice: composition over inheritance, single responsibility, dependency injection (for testability). Saying the principle names scores design points.
Code the skeleton first (classes, method signatures), then fill in. Structure visible early beats perfect details late — interviewers read top-down.

example.walkthrough: LRU in 10 lines: OrderedDict does the ordering work.

lessons.title: Concurrency Questions
concepts: The expected answer: 'GIL means threads don't parallelize CPU-bound work in CPython; use multiprocessing for CPU, threading/asyncio for I/O.' One sentence, then the nuance.
Follow-ups: 'how would you fetch 100 URLs?' (ThreadPoolExecutor or asyncio.gather), 'shared counter race?' (lock or no-sharing), '10k connections?' (asyncio).
Code it: be ready to write the ThreadPoolExecutor fetch and the asyncio.gather fetch live. The pattern should be muscle memory.
Nuance points: pickling costs in multiprocessing, async function coloring, backpressure with semaphores. Depth beyond the one-liner separates candidates.

example.walkthrough: The I/O concurrency answer in 4 lines — have it memorized.

pitfalls: No code ready for fetch patterns.

lessons.title: Final Review and Exam Day
concepts: Review loop: for every mock miss, write the one-line rule ('mutable defaults persist across calls') into the idiom notebook. Re-mock until misses scatter — clustered misses are gaps.
The night before: review the idiom notebook and trap list, no new topics. Sleep beats cramming — problem-solving degrades sharply with fatigue.
Day of: arrive early, warm up with one easy problem (prime the pattern-matching), read each question twice, clarify before coding.
During: narrate, test with examples, state complexity, handle edge cases aloud. The rubric rewards the process — make the process visible.

example.code:
# warm-up: two-sum in 5 minutes, narrated
# 'hash map, one pass, O(n) time' — say it while writing
example.walkthrough: Warm up the voice and the fingers — one easy problem, fully narrated.

simulations.title: The growing list
simulations.brief: A teammate's collect() helper returns a longer list every time it is called with no arguments. The bug report says results 'leak' between calls.

steps.symptom: collect() returns [1] on the first call, [1, 1] on the second, [1, 1, 1] on the third — with no arguments passed.
evidence:
def collect(items=[]):
    items.append(1)
    return items

print(collect())
print(collect())
options: Read the function definition and check when the default value is created
Add a print(items) at the top to watch it grow
Restart the interpreter — it must be caching output
Wrap the call in list() to copy the result
steps.explain: The definition is the crime scene: default arguments are evaluated once at def time, so every call shares the same list object.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: the default list object is created once and mutated on every call.
options: Use None as the default and create a fresh list inside
Call items.clear() at the end of the function
Define the function inside a loop so the default is re-created
steps.explain: The None-sentinel pattern is the standard fix: default None, then `if items is None: items = []` inside the body.

steps.symptom: Fix applied. Verify the behavior is correct.
options: Run collect() twice and confirm both calls return [1]
Check that collect([9]) still returns [9, 1] — callers may pass their own list
Neither — the fix needs no verification
steps.explain: Verify both: no-arg calls return [1] each time, and an explicitly passed list still gets appended to — the fix must not break the parameter's contract.

simulations.debrief: You diagnosed the classic mutable-default-argument bug: defaults evaluate once at def time. The fix is the None sentinel, verified from both the no-arg and explicit-arg paths.

simulations.title: Traceback triage
simulations.brief: Your script just died with a traceback. Work the incident like an on-call engineer: read, localize, fix, verify.

steps.text:
The terminal shows:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "app.py", line 42, in <module>
    total = price * quantity
TypeError: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'str'
What is your FIRST move?

choices.label: Read the last line of the traceback — it names the error and the operation
choices.feedback: Correct instinct: the last line is the diagnosis; the lines above are the trail.

choices.label: Restart the interpreter and rerun
choices.feedback: Restarting clears the evidence. The traceback already tells you what happened.

choices.label: Reinstall Python — the interpreter must be broken
choices.feedback: TypeError is your code's doing, not the interpreter's.

steps.text: `price * quantity` failed because one operand is a str. Which check localizes it fastest?

choices.label: Print type(price) and type(quantity) right before line 42
choices.feedback: type() is the fastest localizer — you see which name holds the string.

choices.label: Wrap line 42 in try/except and move on
choices.feedback: Catching it hides the bug; the str came from somewhere upstream.

choices.label: Convert both with int() and hope
choices.feedback: Blind conversion can raise ValueError on real data. Localize first.

steps.text: `quantity` is the string — it came from input(). What is the correct fix?

choices.label: Convert at the boundary: quantity = int(input(...)) where the data enters
choices.feedback: Fix at the boundary where untrusted text enters. Verify with a rerun.

choices.label: Change line 42 to total = price * int(quantity)
choices.feedback: Works here, but the string-typed variable remains a trap for later code.

simulations.debrief: Traceback triage is: read the last line, localize with type(), fix at the data boundary. You never restart away evidence or paper over a type error with a blind cast.

sections.heading: Language Fundamentals
items: Closures — Closures capture variables by reference, not values.
Late binding — binding the value at definition time — lambda i=i: print(i) — gives each callback its own copy.

Division semantics — floating-point division plus rounding discards the remainder: 100/3 rounds to 33 three times, totaling 99. divmod(100, 3) returns (33, 1), letting you distribute the leftover cent explicitly so the shares always sum to the original total.
String interning — cPython interns some string literals, which is why the check accidentally works in the REPL, but a string parsed from JSON is a distinct object with equal value.
Common trap — string interning is disabled in production.
Common trap — list comprehensions share one lambda object.
Common trap — list multiplication shares one int object.
Common trap — range(5) yields the same object five times.
The — is operator tests whether two names point to the same object in memory. Value comparison with == is the correct test.

sections.heading: Data Structures
items: Idiomatic stdlib — the hand-rolled loop reimplements what the stdlib already provides, tested and optimized.
Memory efficiency — since the pipeline consumes rows exactly once, laziness cuts peak memory from O(n) to O(1) per row.

Dict keys — counter is a dict subclass built exactly for frequency counting; its constructor consumes an iterable and most_common(n) returns the n highest counts without a manual sort. Dict lookup hashes the key, and lists are mutable so Python makes them unhashable —…
Common trap — lists cannot be dict keys on 64-bit Python.
Common trap — dict keys must be strings.
Common trap — list(ids).remove duplicates with a nested loop checking index().
Common trap — read the file in binary mode to halve the memory footprint.

Sets — are unordered by design, so converting through one discards the original sequence. Since Python 3.7 dicts preserve insertion order, dict.fromkeys(ids) keeps the first occurrence of each ID and drops later duplicates, and list() converts back.

items: Function semantics — a transparent wrapper must accept everything the wrapped function accepts. *args captures positional arguments only; without **kwargs, any keyword argument raises TypeError.
Principle — python evaluates default argument expressions once, when the def statement runs.

Common trap — helper modules must be installed with pip before any script can import them.
Common trap — the wrapper must be defined with functools.partial, not a nested def.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Language Fundamentals: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
Redo one Data Structures lab from scratch without looking at the steps.
Recite the key Functions & Modules terms from the glossary aloud from memory.
